name: DevOps for Small Teams
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Developers and architects who ship and run their own products and need production-grade delivery, infrastructure and operations without a dedicated platform team.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of choose-the-setup, read-the-config, incident and cost questions.

domains.name: Delivery: Git workflows and CI/CD
domains.summary: Shipping small changes safely and often: trunk-based development and feature flags, GitHub Actions workflows, caching, reusable workflows and concurrency, secure CI with least-privilege tokens, OIDC and pinned actions, and deployment strategies with migrations and rollback.

domains.name: Containers
domains.summary: Building and running containers well: images, layers, namespaces and cgroups, multi-stage Dockerfiles with good cache order and non-root users, BuildKit cache and secret mounts, Docker Compose for local development, and choosing between Cloud Run, ECS on Fargate or ECS Express Mode and Kubernetes.

domains.name: Infrastructure as code and cloud foundations
domains.summary: Managing cloud resources as reviewed code with Terraform or OpenTofu: modules, remote state with native locking, drift and import, plan and apply in CI, account-per-environment foundations with least-privilege IAM and basic networking, and secrets kept out of code and images.

domains.name: Observability and incident response
domains.summary: Seeing and fixing problems in production: structured logs, metrics and traces with OpenTelemetry, symptom and SLO burn-rate alerts that do not burn people out, synthetic checks and error tracking, small-team incident response and blameless postmortems.

domains.name: Reliability, backups and security operations
domains.summary: Keeping the service up and safe: RPO and RTO with tested restores and point-in-time recovery, health checks, graceful shutdown and zero-downtime deploys, DNS and TLS with ACME certificates and HSTS, supply chain security with SBOMs and provenance, patching and audit logs.

domains.name: Cost and platform choices
domains.summary: Spending money deliberately: how compute, storage, egress and managed services are priced, right-sizing, scale to zero, savings plans, budgets and tags, picking PaaS, containers, serverless or VMs for a tiny team, serverless trade-offs and a minimal internal platform.

scenarios.title: Setting up CI/CD for a new product
scenarios.description: A two-person team starts a new repository. Build a GitHub Actions pipeline with fast tests, cached builds, preview environments, least-privilege tokens and OIDC to the cloud, then release behind feature flags with a safe rollback.

scenarios.title: Containerising and deploying a web app
scenarios.description: Turn a Node or Python app into a small, non-root, multi-stage image with BuildKit caching, run it locally with Compose and healthchecks, and deploy it by digest to Cloud Run or ECS on Fargate.

scenarios.description: Move hand-made cloud resources into Terraform or OpenTofu: import what exists, keep state remote, locked and private, review plans in CI per environment and guard critical resources with prevent_destroy.

scenarios.description: The monthly bill doubled. Find the cost drivers with tags and cost reports, right-size and scale idle services to zero, cut egress, buy savings plans for the steady base and set budget alerts.

lessons.title: Trunk-based development and fast review
lessons.summary: Small teams ship fastest when everyone integrates into one mainline at least daily, hides unfinished work behind flags, and treats code review as a short queue rather than a gate that holds work for days.

sections.heading: Why integrate into the mainline often
sections.body:
Every day a branch lives apart from the mainline, the merge gets larger and riskier. Continuous integration means each developer integrates into the shared mainline at least daily, and every commit on the mainline is built and tested automatically.

**Trunk-based development** is the branching model that follows from that:

- One long-lived branch (`main`). Everything else is short-lived, usually hours to a day or two.
- Small commits that keep the mainline **releasable** at all times.
- A broken mainline build is fixed (or reverted) immediately, because it blocks everyone.

Long-lived feature branches look safe because they isolate work, but they only *delay* the integration pain. The longer the delay, the bigger the conflicts and the less the mainline's tests tell you about the code that will actually ship.

sections.heading: Hiding unfinished work
sections.body:
If you merge daily, some merged code will belong to features that are not finished. Two techniques keep that safe:

1. **Feature flags (release toggles).** The new path ships *off*. The deploy happens now; the release happens later when the flag is flipped.
2. **Branch by abstraction.** Put an interface in front of the code you are replacing, build the new implementation behind it in small merged steps, then switch over and delete the old one.

Release toggles are meant to be **short-lived**. Each one adds a code path to test and reason about, so remove it once the feature is fully rolled out. Flags left in place become *toggle debt*.

sections.heading: Code review that keeps flow fast
sections.body:
Review is often where flow stalls. Practices that keep it moving:

| Problem | Better practice |
|---|---|
| 1,500-line pull requests | Small PRs that do one thing; split refactors from behaviour changes |
| PRs wait days for a reviewer | Treat open reviews as higher priority than starting new work |
| Humans checking style | Linters and formatters in CI, so review is about design and correctness |
| Waiting on many approvers | One knowledgeable approver, plus required status checks |

Fast, automated checks on every PR (lint, unit tests, build) mean the reviewer sees a change that already passes the basics.

keyPoints: Integrate into the mainline at least daily; branches live hours to a day or two.
Keep the mainline releasable; a red mainline build is fixed or reverted first.
Merge unfinished work behind release toggles that default to off, or use branch by abstraction.
Remove release toggles after rollout to avoid toggle debt.
Small PRs, prompt reviews and automated style checks keep review from becoming the bottleneck.

gotchas.trap: Long-lived feature branches reduce risk because they isolate work.
gotchas.correct: They delay integration, so merges grow larger and riskier. Integrate daily and hide unfinished work behind flags.

gotchas.trap: Feature flags are configuration, so they can stay forever.
gotchas.correct: Release toggles should be short-lived. Track them and delete them once the rollout is complete.

gotchas.trap: More required approvers makes review safer.
gotchas.correct: It mostly makes review slower. Pair one knowledgeable reviewer with strong automated checks.

lessons.lab: Take a feature you would normally build on a week-long branch. Plan it as five or more small PRs that each merge to main within a day, with the user-facing path behind a release toggle that defaults to off. Note which PR flips the toggle and which PR deletes it.

lessons.title: GitHub Actions in depth
lessons.summary: Workflows, jobs and steps; matrices for fan-out; caching for dependencies and artifacts for build outputs; reusable workflows for shared pipelines; and concurrency groups to stop runs from overlapping.

sections.heading: Workflows, jobs and steps
sections.body:
A **workflow** is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/` triggered by events (`on:`). It contains **jobs**, which run in parallel on separate runners unless linked with `needs:`. Each job is a list of **steps**: either `run:` shell commands or `uses:` actions.

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "src/**"
      - "!src/**/*.md"
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>
      - run: npm ci && npm test
  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "only runs after every test job passes"
```

Trigger details that catch people out:

- `paths` and `paths-ignore` cannot be combined for the same event. Use `paths` with `!` patterns instead.
- If both `branches` and `paths` are set, **both** must match. Path filters are not evaluated for tag pushes.
- `workflow_dispatch` only appears once the workflow file is on the **default branch**. It accepts up to 25 typed inputs.
- `defaults.run` (shell and working-directory) cannot use expressions.

Runner labels move: `ubuntu-latest` is currently Ubuntu 24.04 even though a 26.04 image exists. Pin a specific label when the OS version matters.

sections.heading: Caching versus artifacts
sections.body:
They solve different problems:

| | Cache | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Reuse dependencies between runs (npm, pip, Go modules) | Pass build outputs between jobs, or keep them after the run |
| Guarantee | Best effort: may be evicted | Kept for the retention period (default 90 days, settable 1–90) |
| Mutability | Immutable per key | Immutable (upload-artifact v4 and later) |

Cache rules worth knowing:

- Default limit 10 GB per repository; entries not accessed for 7 days are evicted, and least-recently-used entries go first at the cap.
- `restore-keys` are tried **in order** as prefix fallbacks. The `cache-hit` output is true **only for an exact `key` match**.
- A run can restore caches from its own branch or the default branch; a PR run can also use its base branch. Sibling feature branches cannot see each other's caches.
- Untrusted triggers that run in the default-branch context (such as `pull_request_target`) get **read-only** cache tokens, which blocks cache poisoning.

Never use the cache to hand a build output to the deploy job: if it was evicted, the deploy has nothing to ship.

sections.heading: Reusable workflows
sections.body:
A reusable workflow declares `on: workflow_call` with inputs and secrets, and a caller uses it at the **job** level with `uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@ref`.

- Up to **10 levels** of nesting and at most **50 unique** reusable workflows per calling file.
- Workflow-level `env` in the caller is **not** propagated to the called workflow. Pass values as `inputs`.
- Permissions can only be **downgraded** down the chain, never raised.

Use reusable workflows for whole pipelines (build, test, deploy) that many repos share; use composite actions for a few steps you repeat inside jobs.

sections.heading: Concurrency groups
sections.body:
`concurrency` makes runs in the same group wait for (or cancel) each other.

```yaml
# PR CI: newer push cancels the superseded run
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

```yaml
# Production deploy: never kill a deploy half way; keep every pending run
concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false
  queue: max
```

- Group names are case-insensitive; expressions may use the `github`, `inputs` and `vars` contexts.
- The `queue` key is new. `single` (the default) keeps at most one pending run, so a newer pending run replaces an older one. `max` keeps up to 100 pending runs in order.
- `queue: max` together with `cancel-in-progress: true` is a **validation error**.

keyPoints: Jobs run in parallel unless linked by needs; steps run in order inside a job.
paths and paths-ignore cannot be combined for one event; branches and paths must both match.
workflow_dispatch only appears when the workflow is on the default branch.
Cache dependencies; use artifacts for build outputs. cache-hit is true only on an exact key match.
Caches are scoped to the branch, the default branch and (for PRs) the base branch.
Reusable workflows: env is not propagated, permissions can only be downgraded, up to 10 nesting levels.
concurrency queue: single keeps one pending run; max keeps up to 100. max with cancel-in-progress true is invalid.

gotchas.trap: A restore-keys fallback restore sets cache-hit to true.
gotchas.correct: cache-hit is true only when the exact key matched. A prefix restore leaves it false.

gotchas.trap: Store the dist folder in the cache so the deploy job can pick it up.
gotchas.correct: Caches can be evicted. Upload an artifact in the build job and download it in the deploy job.

gotchas.trap: Top-level env in the caller is visible inside a reusable workflow.
gotchas.correct: It is not propagated. Pass the values as inputs.

gotchas.trap: With the default concurrency settings, every queued deploy eventually runs.
gotchas.correct: The default queue: single keeps only one pending run; newer pending runs replace older ones. Use queue: max to keep them all.

lessons.lab: Write a workflow with a two-version matrix test job, a build job that uploads an artifact, and a deploy job that downloads it. Add a PR concurrency group that cancels superseded runs and a production group with cancel-in-progress false. Push twice quickly and observe which runs are cancelled or queued.

lessons.title: Securing the CI pipeline
lessons.summary: Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, short-lived OIDC credentials instead of stored cloud keys, actions pinned by commit SHA or a workflow lockfile, and keeping untrusted pull request code away from privileged triggers.

sections.heading: Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN
sections.body:
Set the token to read-only by default and raise permissions only on the jobs that need them.

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  release:
    permissions:
      contents: write   # create the release
```

The rule that surprises people: **if you specify the access for any permission, every permission you did not list is set to `none`.** A job that declares only `id-token: write` therefore loses `contents: read`, and `actions/checkout` of a private repository fails. Shortcuts `read-all`, `write-all` and `{}` (no permissions) also exist.

sections.heading: OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys
sections.body:
Rather than storing an access key in repository secrets, the job requests a short-lived OIDC token from GitHub and exchanges it with the cloud for temporary credentials.

- Issuer: `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`. AWS audience: `sts.amazonaws.com`.
- The job needs `permissions: id-token: write`.
- The cloud role trusts specific **subject (`sub`) claims**, for example `repo:octo-org/octo-repo:environment:prod`, so only that repo and environment can assume it.

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<full-commit-sha>
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/deploy-prod
      aws-region: us-east-1
```

**Immutable subject format.** Repositories created after 2026-07-15 (or that opted in) get a `sub` that includes numeric owner and repo IDs, such as `repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:ref:refs/heads/main`. A trust policy that matches only the name-based form then fails with *Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity*. Update the condition to the ID-based subject.

sections.heading: Pinning actions and workflow lockfiles
sections.body:
A tag such as `@v3` can be moved to malicious code by whoever controls the action repo. Two defences:

1. **Pin to a full-length commit SHA** from the action's own repository (not a fork).
2. **Workflow lockfiles** (GA since 2026-10-28). Install the `github/gh-actions-lock` CLI extension and run `gh actions-lock`; it writes `.github/workflows/actions.lock` covering step-level `uses` and their **transitive** dependencies. GitHub's guidance says a lockfile *supersedes SHA pinning* for repositories that adopt it. Local `./` actions are not locked, and reusable workflows from other repos are covered by those repos' own lockfiles. A "Require lockfile" policy can make lockfiles mandatory.

Keep pins current: Dependabot **alerts** do not cover SHA-pinned actions, but Dependabot **version updates** do update them (and update the lockfile entry in the same PR).

sections.heading: Untrusted code and input
sections.body:
**Script injection.** Values such as a PR title are attacker-controlled. Interpolating them straight into `run:` lets a crafted title execute shell commands. Pass them through `env:` and reference the variable instead:

```yaml
- env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: |
    echo "Title: $TITLE"
```

**`pull_request_target`.** It runs in the context of the base repository's default branch with access to secrets and a write-capable token, even for fork PRs. Checking out and running the PR's code there hands that power to the PR author (a "pwn request"). Guidance:

- Prefer `pull_request` for building untrusted code: fork PRs get no secrets and a read-only token.
- If a privileged step is needed (commenting, labelling, deploying a preview), split it into a `workflow_run` workflow that consumes artifacts but never executes PR code.
- From **2026-12-02**, `pull_request_target` is blocked by default in **public** repositories unless an Actions event policy allows it. Private and internal repos are not affected.

Also: self-hosted runners should almost never be used for public repositories.

keyPoints: Default GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only; listing any permission sets the unlisted ones to none.
Use OIDC with id-token: write and a trust policy scoped to the sub claim instead of stored cloud keys.
New repos get an immutable ID-based sub; name-only trust conditions fail for them.
Pin actions to a full commit SHA from the source repo, or adopt a workflow lockfile (gh actions-lock).
Pass untrusted event fields through env, never directly into run.
Never run untrusted PR code under pull_request_target; it is blocked by default in public repos from 2026-12-02.

gotchas.trap: Adding permissions: id-token: write to a job only adds that one permission.
gotchas.correct: Every unlisted permission becomes none, so add contents: read explicitly if the job checks out a private repo.

gotchas.trap: Pinning to a major tag like v3 protects against a compromised action.
gotchas.correct: Tags are mutable. Pin a full-length commit SHA, or use a workflow lockfile.

gotchas.trap: pull_request_target is the safe way to give fork PRs a secret for tests.
gotchas.correct: It runs with base-repo privileges; executing PR code there exposes secrets. Build with pull_request and split privileged steps into workflow_run.

lessons.lab: Audit one of your workflows: set a top-level read-only permissions block, add per-job grants, replace a stored cloud key with OIDC, pin every action by SHA or generate a lockfile with gh actions-lock, and move any event field used in run into env.

lessons.title: Testing in the pipeline
lessons.summary: Shape the suite as a pyramid, order the pipeline for fast feedback, deal with flaky tests by quarantining and fixing them rather than retrying, and give each pull request its own short-lived preview environment.

sections.heading: The test pyramid
sections.body:
The pyramid is a shape, not a rule about exact counts:

- **Many unit tests** at the bottom: fast, isolated, cheap to run on every commit.
- **Fewer integration or service tests** in the middle: check real interactions with databases, queues and other services.
- **Few end-to-end UI tests** at the top: slow and brittle, so keep them for the critical user journeys.

The usual anti-pattern is the inverted pyramid (or "ice-cream cone"): most coverage is in slow browser tests, so the pipeline takes most of an hour and failures are hard to localise. Push each check down to the lowest level that can catch the bug.

sections.heading: Ordering for fast feedback
sections.body:
Order the pipeline so the cheapest, most likely failures surface first:

1. Lint, type check and unit tests in parallel jobs (minutes).
2. Build and integration tests, gated with `needs:` on step 1.
3. End-to-end tests and the preview deploy.

Use a matrix only where the variation matters, cancel superseded PR runs with a concurrency group, and cache dependencies. A developer should know about most failures within a few minutes of pushing.

sections.heading: Flaky tests
sections.body:
A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Left alone, flakes teach the team to ignore red builds, which destroys the value of the whole suite.

- **Quarantine** the flaky test: move it out of the blocking suite so it cannot hold up merges, and track it so it gets fixed rather than forgotten.
- **Fix the cause**: common sources are shared state between tests, asynchronous waits based on sleeps, dependence on remote services, time and ordering.
- Blanket automatic retries hide the problem; the flake stays, and real intermittent bugs get masked too.

sections.heading: Preview environments per pull request
sections.body:
A preview environment deploys each PR to its own short-lived URL so reviewers and product owners can try the change before merge.

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, closed]
jobs:
  preview:
    if: github.event.action != 'closed'
    environment:
      name: preview
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.url }}
    concurrency:
      group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
      cancel-in-progress: true
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: deploy
        run: ./deploy-preview.sh
  teardown:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./destroy-preview.sh
```

- Tear the environment down when the PR closes, or costs creep up.
- The environment's `url` shows on the PR, so reviewers can click straight through.
- Fork PRs get no secrets under `pull_request`; do not "fix" that by switching to `pull_request_target` and running the PR's code.

keyPoints: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests for critical journeys.
Run lint and unit tests first and gate slower jobs with needs.
Quarantine and fix flaky tests; blanket retries mask real problems.
Preview environments per PR need a teardown on the closed event.

gotchas.trap: End-to-end tests give the most confidence, so most coverage should be there.
gotchas.correct: They are slow and brittle. Cover logic with unit tests and keep end-to-end tests for critical paths.

gotchas.trap: Retrying failed tests three times fixes flakiness.
gotchas.correct: It hides it. Quarantine the test, track it and fix the nondeterminism.

lessons.lab: Measure how long your PR pipeline takes to report its first failure. Reorder it so lint and unit tests run first in parallel, gate the rest with needs, and add a preview deploy job with a teardown job on pull_request closed.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies and rollback
lessons.summary: Rolling, blue-green, canary and feature-flag releases trade cost, speed and blast radius differently; database migrations must stay backward-compatible so a rollback is always possible.

sections.heading: Comparing the strategies
sections.body:
| Strategy | How it works | Strength | Cost or risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rolling | Replace instances a few at a time | No extra full environment; Kubernetes default | Old and new versions serve traffic together during the rollout |
| Blue-green | Run two identical environments; switch the router from blue to green | Near-instant cutover and rollback by switching back | Double capacity during the switch; shared database must suit both |
| Canary | Send a small share of real traffic to the new version, compare metrics, then widen | Smallest blast radius; real-traffic evidence | Needs good metrics and an automatic or quick abort |
| Feature flag | Deploy code dark, then turn it on for chosen users | Release decoupled from deploy; instant kill switch | Flag debt and more code paths to test |

A Kubernetes Deployment uses the `RollingUpdate` strategy by default, tuned with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`. Readiness checks keep traffic off pods that are not ready yet.

sections.heading: Running a canary well
sections.body:
A canary is only useful if you compare it against something:

- Compare canary metrics (error rate, latency) against the current version serving the same kind of traffic, not against a fixed number from last week.
- Start small, and widen in steps only when the canary is healthy.
- Decide the abort criteria **before** the rollout and automate the rollback where you can.

Build the release artifact **once** and promote the same immutable artifact (for a container, the image digest) through staging and production. Rebuilding per environment means production runs something you never tested.

sections.heading: Database migrations in the release flow
sections.body:
During any rolling, canary or blue-green rollout, the old and new code run against **the same database** at the same time. So schema changes must be compatible with both versions.

Use **expand and contract** (also called parallel change):

1. **Expand**: add the new column or table. Old code ignores it.
2. **Migrate**: deploy code that writes both, backfill existing rows, then switch reads to the new structure.
3. **Contract**: once no running version uses the old structure, drop it in a later release.

Renaming or dropping a column in the same deploy as the code change breaks the old version mid-rollout and makes a rollback fail.

sections.heading: Rollback and roll forward
sections.body:
- With Kubernetes, `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` returns to the previous ReplicaSet revision; `kubectl rollout status` watches progress.
- With blue-green, switch the router back to the old environment.
- With a flag, turn the flag off; no deploy needed.
- Code rollback is easy **only if** the schema still supports the previous version. Destructive migrations make "roll forward with a fix" the only option, which is why the contract step waits.

keyPoints: Rolling is the Kubernetes default; old and new versions overlap during the rollout.
Blue-green gives near-instant cutover and rollback at the cost of double capacity.
Canary limits blast radius; compare against the current version and define abort criteria first.
Feature flags decouple deploy from release and act as a kill switch.
Use expand and contract so every migration works with both the old and the new code.
Build once and promote the same artifact through environments.

gotchas.trap: Blue-green means the database problem goes away because there are two environments.
gotchas.correct: Both usually share one database, so schema changes must still be backward-compatible.

gotchas.trap: Rename the column in the same release as the code that uses the new name.
gotchas.correct: The old version breaks mid-rollout. Expand, migrate, and contract in a later release.

gotchas.trap: Rebuild the image for production from the same commit; it is the same thing.
gotchas.correct: Promote the exact artifact (image digest) that passed staging.

lessons.lab: Plan the rename of a users.fullname column to display_name as three releases using expand and contract. For each release, write which code version can be rolled back safely and what the rollback command or action is.

lessons.title: Container fundamentals: images, layers, namespaces and cgroups
lessons.summary: What a container actually is on a Linux host, how images are built from immutable layers, and when a VM is still the better isolation boundary.

sections.heading: A container is a process, not a machine
sections.body:
A container is an ordinary process on the host that the kernel has wrapped in isolation. Docker's overview puts it this way: Docker "uses a technology called namespaces to provide the isolated workspace called the container", and each aspect of a container runs in a separate namespace with access limited to it.

Two kernel features do the work:

- **Namespaces** decide what the process can *see*: its own process tree (PID), network stack (NET), mount table (MNT), hostname (UTS), IPC objects and, optionally, user IDs (USER).
- **Control groups (cgroups)** decide what the process can *use*. Docker's security page describes them as implementing resource accounting and limiting, so each container gets its fair share of memory, CPU and disk I/O.

So `docker run --memory=512m` is a cgroup setting, and the fact that `ps` inside the container shows only a handful of processes is the PID namespace.

sections.heading: Images and layers
sections.body:
An image is a stack of **read-only layers** plus metadata (entrypoint, env, user, exposed ports). Each filesystem-changing instruction in a Dockerfile (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) produces a layer. Layers are content-addressed and shared: ten images built from the same base store that base once.

When a container starts, the runtime adds a thin **writable layer** on top. Writes go there using copy-on-write. Two consequences matter in practice:

1. Deleting a file in a later layer only hides it. If a secret was copied in one layer and `rm`'d in the next, it is still in the image and anyone who pulls it can extract it.
2. The writable layer disappears with the container. Data you need to keep belongs in a volume or an external store, never in the container filesystem.

sections.heading: Containers vs virtual machines
sections.body:
A VM virtualises hardware and boots its own kernel. A container shares the **host kernel**, which is why it starts in milliseconds and has little overhead, and also why its isolation boundary is weaker: a kernel vulnerability is shared by every container on the host.

| | Container | VM |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel | Shared with host | Own guest kernel |
| Start time | Sub-second | Seconds to minutes |
| Isolation | Namespaces, cgroups, seccomp, capabilities | Hypervisor |
| OS mix | Linux containers need a Linux kernel | Any guest OS |

Rule of thumb: containers are the packaging and deployment unit; when you need a hard multi-tenant boundary (untrusted code from different customers), put a VM or micro-VM boundary underneath. Many managed container platforms add a sandbox of this kind between customers for you.

keyPoints: Namespaces limit what a process sees; cgroups limit what it can consume.
Image layers are read-only and shared; the container adds one writable copy-on-write layer.
A file removed in a later layer still exists in the earlier layer.
Containers share the host kernel, so they are lighter than VMs but a weaker isolation boundary.
Container filesystem writes are lost when the container is removed; use volumes or external storage.

gotchas.trap: "I deleted the key with rm in the next RUN, so the image is clean."
gotchas.correct: The earlier layer still contains the key. Use a BuildKit secret mount so it never lands in a layer.

gotchas.trap: "Containers are lightweight VMs."
gotchas.correct: They are isolated host processes sharing one kernel; no guest kernel is booted.

gotchas.trap: "Memory limits are a namespace feature."
gotchas.correct: Resource limits are cgroups. Namespaces only isolate visibility.

lessons.lab: Run `docker run --rm -it --memory=64m alpine sh`, then run `ps` and `hostname` inside it and compare with the host. Run `docker history` on an image you built and find the layer that added the most bytes.

lessons.title: Writing good Dockerfiles
lessons.summary: Multi-stage builds, cache-friendly instruction order, .dockerignore, small trusted base images, non-root users and correct signal handling.

sections.heading: Order instructions for the cache
sections.body:
BuildKit reuses a cached layer until an instruction or its inputs change; after that, every later step reruns. Put what changes least first. For a Node app, copy the dependency manifests, install, *then* copy source:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

Editing a source file now invalidates only the final `COPY`, not the dependency install. The same pattern applies to `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `requirements.txt` and so on. The `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` line pins the frontend to the latest stable 1.x.

sections.heading: Multi-stage builds
sections.body:
Compilers, dev dependencies and test tools are needed to *build*, not to *run*. A multi-stage build keeps them in an earlier stage and copies only the output into a small runtime stage:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER 65532:65532
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

Smaller images pull faster, start faster on scale-out and carry fewer packages to patch. You can target an intermediate stage with `docker build --target build` for tests.

sections.heading: .dockerignore and the build context
sections.body:
Everything in the build context is sent to the builder. Without a `.dockerignore`, that includes `.git`, local `node_modules`, build output and often `.env` files. That slows every build, busts the cache when irrelevant files change, and risks a `COPY . .` baking credentials into the image.

```text
.git
node_modules
dist
.env*
*.log
```

sections.heading: Base images, updates and users
sections.body:
Docker's best-practices guide recommends:

- **Trusted, small bases**: Docker Official Images, Verified Publisher or DSOS images; slim or distroless variants where possible. Docker Hardened Images are another minimal option.
- **Pin by digest** (`FROM node:22-slim@sha256:...`) for reproducibility, and let Dependabot's `docker` ecosystem open PRs to bump the digest.
- **Rebuild regularly with `--pull`** so you pick up patched base layers (add `--no-cache` for a fully fresh build).
- **Combine `apt-get update && apt-get install`** in one `RUN` so a cached, stale `update` layer is never reused; sort multi-line package lists.
- **Run as non-root**: create a user with an explicit UID/GID and switch with `USER`. Use an absolute `WORKDIR`.

sections.heading: PID 1 and signals
sections.body:
`docker stop` sends `STOPSIGNAL` (SIGTERM by default) to PID 1, waits, then sends SIGKILL. In **shell form** (`ENTRYPOINT node server.js`) the process runs under `/bin/sh -c`, is not PID 1, and never sees SIGTERM, so it is killed without a graceful shutdown. Use **exec form** (`ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]`), or make a wrapper script finish with `exec` so the app replaces the shell. If the app cannot reap zombie children, add an init (Compose `init: true`).

Also remember: `ARG` values are not present in the final image, but `ENV` values persist in it, and neither is safe for secrets.

keyPoints: Copy dependency manifests and install before copying the rest of the source.
Multi-stage builds keep toolchains out of the runtime image.
A .dockerignore keeps .git, node_modules and .env files out of the context.
Pin base images by digest, automate bumps, and rebuild with --pull.
Run as a non-root USER with an explicit UID/GID.
Use exec-form ENTRYPOINT/CMD so the app is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM.

gotchas.trap: `COPY . .` as the first instruction after FROM.
gotchas.correct: Copy manifests, install dependencies, then copy source so code edits do not reinstall everything.

gotchas.trap: `RUN apt-get update` and `RUN apt-get install -y curl` as separate instructions.
gotchas.correct: Combine them in one RUN so the package index is never a stale cached layer.

gotchas.trap: Shell-form `ENTRYPOINT` with an app that handles SIGTERM.
gotchas.correct: Shell form runs under /bin/sh -c; the app is not PID 1 and never gets the signal. Use exec form.

gotchas.trap: Assuming files copied without --chown belong to the app user.
gotchas.correct: Copied files are owned by 0:0 unless you pass --chown (numeric IDs when combined with --link).

lessons.lab: Take an existing single-stage Dockerfile, convert it to multi-stage with a non-root USER, add a .dockerignore, and compare `docker image ls` sizes and rebuild time after editing one source file.

lessons.title: BuildKit: cache mounts, secrets, multi-platform and digests
lessons.summary: Use BuildKit mounts to speed builds and keep secrets out of layers, build for amd64 and arm64, share cache in CI, and deploy by immutable digest.

sections.heading: Cache mounts
sections.body:
A cache mount gives a `RUN` step a persistent directory that survives between builds but is **not** written into the image:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
```

Typical targets: npm `/root/.npm`, pip `/root/.cache/pip`, Go `/go/pkg/mod` and `/root/.cache/go-build`. `sharing` is `shared` by default; apt needs `locked`. Important limit: cache mounts live on the builder and are **not** included in exported build cache, so on ephemeral CI runners they start empty unless the builder persists.

sections.heading: Exported cache for CI
sections.body: To reuse *layer* cache across CI runs, export it with `--cache-to` and import with `--cache-from`. Backends include `inline`, `registry`, `local` and `gha` (GitHub Actions cache, still marked beta). `mode=min` (the default) exports only the layers of the final image; `mode=max` also exports intermediate stages, which is what makes multi-stage builds cache well. The default `docker` driver supports only some backends; a `docker-container` builder (via `docker/setup-buildx-action`) supports them all.

sections.heading: Secret mounts
sections.body:
Never pass credentials through `ARG` or `ENV`; both end up recorded in the image. Mount them for one step instead:

```bash
docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc .
docker build --secret id=token,env=GH_TOKEN .
```

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token,env=GH_TOKEN ./fetch-private-deps.sh
```

By default a secret appears at `/run/secrets/<id>`. `--mount=type=ssh` forwards an SSH agent for private Git dependencies.

sections.heading: Multi-platform builds
sections.body:
```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t registry.example.com/app:1.4.2 --push .
```

Docker Engine 29 and later, and Docker Desktop, use the containerd image store by default, which can hold multi-platform images locally; on older engines use a `docker-container` builder and push. Three strategies:

1. **QEMU emulation**: easiest, but slow for compile-heavy builds.
2. **Native nodes**: one builder per architecture.
3. **Cross-compilation**: run the compiler on the build platform and target the other, using the `BUILDPLATFORM`, `TARGETOS` and `TARGETARCH` build arguments. Usually the fastest for Go and Rust:

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.25 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/app .
```

sections.heading: Tags, digests and attestations
sections.body:
A **tag** (`app:1.4.2`, `app:latest`) is a mutable pointer: anyone with push rights can move it. A **digest** (`app@sha256:...`) identifies exact content and cannot change. Good practice:

- Tag each build with something traceable (git SHA, semver) and avoid deploying `latest`.
- Have CI record the pushed digest and deploy **by digest**, so staging and production run byte-identical images and rollbacks are exact.
- BuildKit attaches **provenance** attestations (`mode=min`) by default; add `--sbom=true` for an SBOM and `--provenance=mode=max` for full provenance.

keyPoints: Cache mounts speed package installs but are not part of exported cache.
Use --cache-to/--cache-from with mode=max to cache intermediate stages in CI.
Secrets go through --secret and RUN --mount=type=secret, never ARG or ENV.
Cross-compile with FROM --platform=BUILDPLATFORM instead of emulating compile-heavy builds.
Tags move; digests do not. Deploy by digest.
Provenance attestations are attached by default; SBOM is opt-in.

gotchas.trap: "Our GitHub cache export includes the npm cache mount."
gotchas.correct: Cache mounts are not exported; only layer cache is. Persist the builder or accept a cold mount.

gotchas.trap: `ARG NPM_TOKEN` for a private registry, since "ARG is not in the final image".
gotchas.correct: The value is still recorded in image metadata and history. Use a secret mount.

gotchas.trap: Promoting `app:latest` from staging to production.
gotchas.correct: Promote the digest staging tested; a tag may have moved in between.

lessons.lab: Add a secret mount for a private registry token and an npm cache mount to a Dockerfile. Build for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 with buildx, push, and inspect the manifest list with `docker buildx imagetools inspect` to see each platform digest.

lessons.title: Local development with Docker Compose
lessons.summary: Model a local stack as Compose services with networks, volumes, healthchecks and depends_on conditions, and avoid the common port and startup traps.

sections.heading: A modern compose.yaml
sections.body:
The top-level `version` key is **obsolete**: Compose ignores it apart from a warning. A minimal app plus database:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s
volumes:
  pgdata:
```

sections.heading: Networks and ports
sections.body:
Compose creates a default network named `<project>_default`. Each service is reachable by its **service name** via DNS, on its **container port**. So `web` talks to `db:5432`, regardless of any host port mapping, and `localhost` inside `web` means the `web` container itself.

`ports` uses `[HOST:]CONTAINER[/PROTOCOL]`. Without a host IP, the port binds to **0.0.0.0**, exposing it on every interface of your laptop. For a database that only other services use, publish nothing; if you need a local client, bind to `127.0.0.1`.

sections.heading: Startup order and healthchecks
sections.body:
Short-form `depends_on: [db]` only orders container **creation/start**; it does not wait for the database to accept connections. The long form takes a `condition`:

- `service_started` (the short-form behaviour)
- `service_healthy`: waits until the dependency's healthcheck passes
- `service_completed_successfully`: waits for a one-shot job, such as migrations, to exit 0

`restart: true` restarts the dependent when the dependency is restarted, and `required: false` lets the stack start if an optional dependency is absent. A list-form `healthcheck.test` must start with `CMD`, `CMD-SHELL` or `NONE`.

sections.heading: Volumes, env and lifecycle details
sections.body:
- **Named volumes** (`pgdata:`) persist across `docker compose down`; `down -v` deletes them. Bind mounts (`./src:/app/src`) are for live code reload.
- In an `env_file` list the last file wins, and `environment:` overrides `env_file`.
- Compose **secrets** mount at `/run/secrets/<name>`. **Profiles** let optional services (a debugger, a queue UI) start only when requested.
- On stop, Compose waits `stop_grace_period` (10s by default) after SIGTERM before SIGKILL; `init: true` adds an init process as PID 1.

keyPoints: Drop the top-level version key; it is obsolete.
Services reach each other by service name on the container port.
Ports without a host IP bind to 0.0.0.0; bind local-only tools to 127.0.0.1.
Use depends_on with condition: service_healthy plus a healthcheck to wait for readiness.
Use service_completed_successfully for one-shot migration jobs.
Named volumes survive down; down -v removes them.

gotchas.trap: `DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5433/app` inside the web container because the host maps 5433:5432.
gotchas.correct: Use `db:5432`: the service name and the container port.

gotchas.trap: Short-form depends_on and then wondering why the app crashes on boot.
gotchas.correct: It only waits for the container to start. Add a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy.

gotchas.trap: `ports: ["5432:5432"]` on a laptop on café Wi-Fi.
gotchas.correct: That binds to all interfaces. Omit ports or use 127.0.0.1:5432:5432.

lessons.lab: Write a compose.yaml with web, db and a one-shot migrate service. Make web depend on db (service_healthy) and migrate (service_completed_successfully). Break the healthcheck on purpose and watch `docker compose up` hold web back.

lessons.title: Running containers in production: managed platforms vs Kubernetes
lessons.summary: Choose between managed container platforms such as Cloud Run and Amazon ECS (Express Mode or Fargate) and Kubernetes, and meet the runtime contract either way.

sections.heading: The managed options
sections.body:
For a small team, the default answer for a stateless HTTP service is a managed container platform where you hand over an image and get scaling, TLS and load balancing:

- **Google Cloud Run**: deploy an image, scale on requests (including to zero), per-instance concurrency (default 80, configurable up to 1,000).
- **Amazon ECS Express Mode**: one call with an image and two IAM roles provisions ECS on Fargate, an Application Load Balancer, auto scaling and networking; there is no extra charge beyond the underlying resources. Plain **ECS on Fargate** gives more control with no servers to manage.
- **Fly-style platforms**: push an image, run it close to users, minimal configuration.

**AWS App Runner is closed to new customers.** Existing users can keep running it, but AWS plans no new features and points new workloads at ECS Express Mode. Treat App Runner as legacy.

sections.heading: The runtime contract
sections.body:
Managed platforms expect a well-behaved container. Cloud Run's contract is a good checklist that applies almost everywhere:

- **Listen on `0.0.0.0` and the port given in the PORT environment variable** (8080 by default). Binding to `127.0.0.1` fails health checks.
- **Handle SIGTERM**: Cloud Run sends SIGTERM, waits 10 seconds, then SIGKILL. Kubernetes runs any preStop hook, sends SIGTERM and waits the pod's termination grace period before SIGKILL.
- **Treat the filesystem as ephemeral**: on Cloud Run it is in memory, counts against the instance's memory and is lost when the instance stops. Put state in a database or object storage.
- **Stay stateless** between requests so any instance can serve any request.

sections.heading: When Kubernetes is worth it
sections.body:
Kubernetes is a powerful, portable control plane: self-healing, declarative rollouts, service discovery, and an enormous ecosystem. It also carries real operating cost: the cluster, its add-ons (ingress, cert management, autoscaling, observability) and **upgrades**. The project ships a new minor roughly three times a year and supports only the three most recent minors, so a cluster that is not upgraded regularly falls out of support within about a year.

This is a judgment call, not a rule from any vendor. Signals that Kubernetes is worth it:

- Many services with shared platform needs and a team (or budget) to own the platform.
- Workloads managed platforms handle poorly: custom schedulers, GPUs with specific sharing, long-running stateful systems, sidecars and operators.
- A hard portability requirement across clouds or on-premises.

Signals it is not: a handful of stateless services, one or two engineers on call, and no one who wants to own cluster upgrades. Start managed; migrating a well-behaved container later is cheap.

keyPoints: Managed container platforms are the default for small teams running stateless services.
App Runner is closed to new customers; use ECS Express Mode or ECS on Fargate on AWS.
Listen on 0.0.0.0 and the PORT variable; handle SIGTERM within the grace window.
Cloud Run filesystem writes are in-memory and lost when the instance stops.
Kubernetes pays off with many services, unusual workloads or portability needs, and costs ongoing upgrade work.

gotchas.trap: Choosing App Runner for a new AWS account because it is "the simple one".
gotchas.correct: It is closed to new customers. Use ECS Express Mode or ECS on Fargate.

gotchas.trap: Writing uploads to /tmp on Cloud Run and serving them later.
gotchas.correct: The filesystem is in-memory and per instance; use object storage.

gotchas.trap: Standing up a self-managed Kubernetes cluster for one API and a worker.
gotchas.correct: A managed platform covers this with far less operational load.

lessons.lab: Deploy the same image to Cloud Run (or ECS Express Mode). Make the app log when it receives SIGTERM, deploy a new revision, and confirm in logs that in-flight requests finish before shutdown.

lessons.title: Terraform and OpenTofu building blocks
lessons.summary: Providers, resources, variables, outputs and modules: the pieces of an infrastructure-as-code configuration, and how to structure them so dev, staging and prod stay consistent.

sections.heading: Why infrastructure as code
sections.body:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means the shape of your cloud lives in reviewed text files rather than in someone's memory of console clicks. For a small team the payoff is concrete:

- **Reproducibility.** Staging and prod are built from the same code, so "works in staging" means something.
- **Review.** A pull request shows exactly which security group rule or database setting changes.
- **Recovery.** If an account or region is lost, the configuration plus your backups is the rebuild plan.

Terraform and OpenTofu share the same HCL language and workflow (`init`, `plan`, `apply`). OpenTofu is an open-source (MPL 2.0) fork that is a CNCF project; Terraform moved to the Business Source License in version 1.6. For writing configurations the concepts below are the same in both tools.

sections.heading: Providers and resources
Variables, locals and outputs
sections.body:
- **Input variables** (`variable` blocks) are a module's parameters. Give them a `type`, a `description` and, where it helps, a `validation` rule. Values come from `*.tfvars` files, `-var` flags or `TF_VAR_name` environment variables.
- **Locals** name an expression you would otherwise repeat, such as a common tag map.
- **Outputs** (`output` blocks) expose values from a module: to the caller of a child module, or to the CLI and other tooling from a root module.

Marking a variable or output `sensitive = true` hides it from CLI output only. The value is still written to state, which is covered in the next lesson.

sections.heading: Modules
sections.body:
Every configuration is a module: the directory you run Terraform in is the **root module**, and it can call **child modules** with `module` blocks.

```hcl
module "network" {
  source     = "../../modules/network"
  cidr_block = "10.20.0.0/16"
  az_count   = 2
}

resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "db" {
  name       = "app-db"
  subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids
}
```

A caller can only read what the child module declares as an output (`module.network.private_subnet_ids`), never the child's internal resources directly. That boundary is the point: a module is an interface.

A good small-team layout is one shared module per building block (network, database, service) and one thin root configuration per environment that calls those modules with different variables. Avoid modules that wrap a single resource with no added opinion; they add indirection without reuse.

keyPoints: Providers are API plugins; resources are the objects they manage.
Commit .terraform.lock.hcl so provider versions are pinned and upgrades are reviewed.
Variables are inputs, locals are named expressions, outputs are the module interface.
A caller reads a child module only through its outputs.
Use shared modules plus a thin root configuration per environment.

gotchas.trap: sensitive = true keeps a value out of state.
gotchas.correct: It only redacts CLI output; the value is still stored in state and plan files.

gotchas.trap: Reference a child module resource directly, for example module.db.aws_db_instance.this.address.
gotchas.correct: Declare an output in the child module and reference module.db.<output_name>.

gotchas.trap: Add .terraform.lock.hcl to .gitignore.
gotchas.correct: Commit it so every run uses the same provider versions and checksums.

lessons.lab: Write a small module that creates an S3 bucket with versioning and outputs its ARN. Call it from two root configurations (dev and prod) with different bucket names, run terraform init and terraform plan in each, and commit the generated .terraform.lock.hcl.

lessons.title: State, locking, drift and import
lessons.summary: Why Terraform keeps state, how to store and lock it remotely, why the state file is a secret, and how to handle drift, imports and resources you stop managing.

sections.heading: What state is
sections.body:
State maps each resource address in your configuration (`aws_s3_bucket.assets`) to a real object ID in the cloud, along with its last known attributes. Terraform compares configuration, state and the real world to build a plan. Without state it cannot know that a bucket it sees is "its" bucket.

A local `terraform.tfstate` file works for one person experimenting. A team needs **remote state** so everyone and CI see the same mapping, plus **locking** so two applies cannot write it at once.

sections.heading: Remote state on S3 with native locking
sections.body:
```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "example-tfstate"
    key          = "prod/network.tfstate"
    region       = "us-east-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

- `use_lockfile = true` turns on S3-native locking with a `.tflock` object next to the state.
- DynamoDB-based locking (`dynamodb_table`) is **deprecated** and will be removed in a future minor version. Do not build new setups on it.
- The docs strongly recommend **bucket versioning**, so a bad write can be rolled back.
- The CI role needs `s3:ListBucket`, Get/Put on the state object, and Get/Put/Delete on the lock object.

If a run dies and leaves a lock behind, `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID` releases it. Use it only after confirming nobody else is running, because unlocking someone else's live lock allows two writers.

sections.heading: State files are secrets
sections.body:
Terraform stores resource attributes **in plain text** in state and in saved plan files, including database passwords and generated keys. `sensitive = true` only redacts CLI output, and `terraform output -json` still prints sensitive values.

Treat state like a credential store:

- Keep it in a private, encrypted, versioned bucket with tight IAM access. Never commit it to Git, even a private repo.
- Prefer patterns that keep secrets out of state entirely: **ephemeral values** are omitted from state and plan, and **write-only arguments** (`*_wo` with a `*_wo_version` to trigger updates) need Terraform 1.11 or later. Letting the database service generate and store its own master password in a secret manager also keeps it out of state.
- **OpenTofu only:** client-side state encryption in a `terraform { encryption { ... } }` block (or `TF_ENCRYPTION`), with key providers such as `aws_kms`, `gcp_kms` or `pbkdf2` and the `aes_gcm` method. It can also encrypt plans, supports a `fallback` block for key rotation and `enforced = true`. Losing the key means losing the state. Terraform has no equivalent client-side encryption.

sections.heading: Drift, import, moved and removed
sections.body:
**Drift** is when the real world no longer matches state, usually from a console change during an incident.

- A normal `terraform plan` refreshes and proposes changes to put reality back to the configuration.
- `terraform plan -refresh-only` (and `apply -refresh-only`) only updates state and outputs to match reality, without changing infrastructure. Use it to accept a change, then update the code so the next normal plan is clean.

**Adopting existing objects:** an `import` block brings a hand-made resource under management through the normal plan and review flow.

```hcl
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy
  id = "legacy-uploads-bucket"
}
```

`terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` writes a starting resource block for you to tidy.

**Renaming:** a `moved` block records that a resource changed address (for example into a module), so Terraform updates state instead of destroying and recreating it.

**Letting go:** a `removed` block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` drops a resource from state but leaves the real object running. Just deleting the resource block would plan a destroy.

keyPoints: State maps configuration addresses to real object IDs; teams need it remote and locked.
S3 backend: use_lockfile = true; DynamoDB locking is deprecated. Turn on bucket versioning.
State and saved plans hold secrets in plain text; sensitive only hides CLI output.
plan -refresh-only accepts drift into state without touching infrastructure.
import adopts, moved renames, removed with destroy = false lets go without deleting.
Client-side state encryption is an OpenTofu feature; losing its key loses the state.

gotchas.trap: New S3 backends should add a DynamoDB table for locking.
gotchas.correct: Use use_lockfile = true; DynamoDB locking is deprecated.

gotchas.trap: encrypt = true on the S3 backend means only Terraform can read the state.
gotchas.correct: It is server-side encryption; anyone with read access to the object still gets plaintext. Restrict IAM, or use OpenTofu client-side encryption.

gotchas.trap: Delete the resource block to stop managing something.
gotchas.correct: Deleting the block plans a destroy. Use a removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false }.

gotchas.trap: Fix a stuck lock by deleting the state file.
gotchas.correct: Confirm no run is active, then use force-unlock with the lock ID.

lessons.lab: Create an S3 bucket with versioning for state, configure the S3 backend with use_lockfile = true, and run two applies at once to see the lock error. Then create a bucket by hand in the console, adopt it with an import block and plan -generate-config-out, and finally drop it from management with a removed block and destroy = false.

lessons.title: Plan and apply safely in CI
lessons.summary: A pull-request plan and approved-apply pipeline, isolating environments, keeping cloud credentials short-lived, and the lifecycle settings that prevent destroy surprises.

sections.heading: The plan-review-apply loop
sections.body:
A safe pipeline for a small team:

1. On every pull request, CI runs `terraform plan` with a read-only role and posts the summary for review.
2. Reviewers read the plan, not just the code diff. The count line ("N to add, N to change, N to destroy") and every "must be replaced" entry deserve attention.
3. After merge, CI runs `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, a protected environment requires approval, and `terraform apply tfplan` applies **exactly** that saved plan.

Applying a saved plan file means no new decisions happen between review and apply. If the state changed in between, Terraform refuses the stale plan. Remember that saved plan files contain the same plaintext values as state, so treat CI artifacts that hold them as secrets.

sections.heading: Environments: separate backends, not just workspaces
sections.body:
CLI **workspaces** let one configuration keep several state files in the **same backend**. The Terraform docs say they are not a suitable isolation mechanism when environments need separate credentials and access controls.

For staging and prod, use **separate root configurations** (for example `envs/staging` and `envs/prod`) that call shared modules, each with **its own backend** and, ideally, in its own cloud account. Then a mistake in staging credentials cannot touch prod state, and prod applies can require a different approval.

Workspaces still fit short-lived copies of the same environment, such as a per-branch test stack.

sections.heading: Credentials for CI
sections.body:
Do not store long-lived cloud access keys in CI secrets. In GitHub Actions, grant the job `id-token: write` and exchange the OIDC token for a short-lived role session (on AWS, `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` via `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`).

Scope the role's trust policy on the token's `sub` claim. A prod apply role can trust only `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:prod`, and the `prod` GitHub environment can require reviewers, so the role is assumable only after approval. Repositories created after 2026-07-15 (or that opted in) emit an immutable `sub` with numeric IDs, such as `repo:ORG@123456/REPO@456789:environment:prod`; a name-only trust condition then fails with "Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", so match the format your repository actually sends. Give the plan job a separate read-only role.

sections.heading: Avoiding destroy surprises with lifecycle
sections.body:
The `lifecycle` meta-argument changes how Terraform handles a resource:

- `prevent_destroy = true` makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail with an error. It **does not** help if someone deletes the resource block itself, because the setting goes with the block.
- `create_before_destroy = true` builds the replacement before removing the old object when an argument forces replacement, which avoids a gap for things like certificates or launch templates.
- `ignore_changes` tells Terraform to ignore changes to listed attributes that something else manages (for example an autoscaler's desired count).
- `replace_triggered_by` forces replacement when a referenced resource or attribute changes.

Lifecycle arguments take **literal values only**: you cannot set `prevent_destroy = var.is_prod`.

Two more guards: a `moved` block for refactors (so a rename is not a destroy and create), and a habit of stopping the pipeline whenever a prod plan shows an unexpected destroy or replace.

keyPoints: Plan on PRs; after approval, apply the exact saved plan file.
Read destroy counts and "must be replaced" lines in every prod plan.
Workspaces share one backend; use separate root configs and backends per environment.
CI uses OIDC to assume short-lived roles; scope prod trust to the prod environment.
prevent_destroy blocks destroy plans but not removal of the resource block.
Lifecycle arguments accept literal values only.

gotchas.trap: Use terraform.workspace conditionals to keep prod and staging isolated.
gotchas.correct: Workspaces share a backend and credentials; use separate backends, configs and ideally accounts.

gotchas.trap: Set prevent_destroy = var.protect so only prod is protected.
gotchas.correct: Lifecycle settings take literal values; set it in the prod-facing module or configuration directly.

gotchas.trap: Run apply -auto-approve on merge, re-planning from scratch.
gotchas.correct: Apply the saved plan file that reviewers approved.

lessons.lab: Build a GitHub Actions workflow that runs terraform plan on pull requests with a read-only OIDC role, and on push to main saves a plan, waits for approval on a prod environment, and applies the saved plan. Add prevent_destroy to a test bucket and confirm a destroy plan fails.

lessons.title: Cloud foundations for small teams
lessons.summary: Accounts per environment, least-privilege IAM, a simple VPC with public and private subnets, security groups, and managed databases, with the cost traps to avoid.

sections.heading: Accounts or projects per environment
sections.body:
The strongest isolation boundary in a cloud is the **account** (AWS) or **project** (Google Cloud). Even a tiny team benefits from at least separate prod and non-prod accounts:

- A leaked dev credential cannot touch prod data.
- Billing, quotas and budgets are clear per environment.
- Guardrails can differ per account.

On AWS, group accounts under **AWS Organizations**. **Service control policies (SCPs)** and resource control policies (RCPs) set the maximum permissions in an account, for example denying regions you do not use. They **grant nothing by themselves**; identities still need IAM policies.

sections.heading: IAM least privilege
sections.body:
The AWS IAM best practices boil down to a few rules:

- **People** sign in through federation (IAM Identity Center or an external IdP) and get **temporary credentials**. Avoid IAM users with long-lived access keys. Require MFA, preferably phishing-resistant passkeys or security keys.
- **Workloads** use **roles**: an instance or task role inside AWS, OIDC web identity federation for CI outside AWS.
- Grant **least privilege**. Start from what a workload actually does, and use IAM Access Analyzer to generate and validate policies.
- Use **permissions boundaries** when you let developers create roles, so a delegated role can never exceed the boundary.

sections.heading: Networking basics: VPC, subnets, security groups
sections.body:
A typical small-team VPC spans two or more Availability Zones:

- **Public subnets** have a route to an internet gateway. Put load balancers (and NAT gateways, if you need them) here.
- **Private subnets** have no direct internet route. Put app tasks and databases here. Outbound internet access from a private subnet needs a NAT device.
- **Security groups** are stateful virtual firewalls on each network interface. You write **allow rules only**, and return traffic is allowed automatically. A rule's source can be **another security group**, so "database allows 5432 from the app security group" keeps working as app instances come and go.

Cost traps to design around (check current rates on the pricing pages):

- A **NAT gateway** is billed per hour and per GB processed, so a NAT per AZ for a quiet dev environment adds up.
- **Public IPv4 addresses** are billed hourly whether in use or idle.
- **Gateway endpoints** for S3 and DynamoDB have no additional charge, and they keep that traffic off the NAT gateway.

sections.heading: Managed databases
sections.body:
For a small team a managed database (Amazon RDS or Aurora, Cloud SQL, Supabase-style hosted Postgres) is almost always better than running Postgres on a VM. The provider handles patching, backups and failover.

- Put the database in **private subnets**, reachable only from the app's security group.
- Turn on **Multi-AZ** for prod. A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment keeps a standby in another AZ for automatic failover. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two standbys that can also serve reads.
- Use automated backups and point-in-time recovery, and test restores.
- Let RDS **manage the master user password in Secrets Manager** rather than passing it through Terraform variables.

Manage all of this in Terraform, with `prevent_destroy` on the prod database resource.

keyPoints: Separate accounts or projects per environment are the strongest isolation.
SCPs and RCPs are guardrails; they grant no permissions.
People federate with temporary credentials and MFA; workloads and CI use roles.
Databases and app tasks live in private subnets; security groups reference each other.
NAT gateways and public IPv4 cost money while idle; S3 gateway endpoints are free.
Prod databases: managed, Multi-AZ, backups tested, password managed by the service.

gotchas.trap: An SCP that allows s3:* gives everyone in the account S3 access.
gotchas.correct: SCPs only limit; IAM policies must still grant the permission.

gotchas.trap: Open the database port to 0.0.0.0/0 and rely on a strong password.
gotchas.correct: Keep it in a private subnet and allow only the app security group as the source.

gotchas.trap: Security groups need explicit deny rules for unwanted traffic.
gotchas.correct: Security groups support allow rules only; anything not allowed is dropped.

lessons.lab: Write a network module with two public and two private subnets, an S3 gateway endpoint, and security groups where the database group allows Postgres only from the app group. Add an RDS instance in the private subnets with Multi-AZ, a Secrets Manager-managed master password and prevent_destroy.

lessons.title: Secrets and configuration
lessons.summary: Twelve-factor config, secret managers, rotation, and why secrets never belong in images, repos or Terraform state.

sections.heading: Twelve-factor config
sections.body:
The Twelve-Factor App's config factor says: **store config in the environment**. Config is everything that varies between deploys (database URLs, API keys, feature switches), and it must be strictly separated from code. A good test: could you open-source the repo right now without leaking a credential?

The practical result is **build once, deploy many**: one image is promoted from staging to prod, and each environment injects its own configuration at runtime. Building a separate image per environment with config baked in breaks that, and means the artifact you tested is not the one you ship.

sections.heading: Secret managers
sections.body:
Environment variables are the interface, but secrets should be **stored** in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Google Cloud Secret Manager) and injected at deploy or start-up time:

- Access is controlled per secret with IAM, and reads are audited.
- The application or platform fetches the value at runtime, so it is never in the image, the repo or a CI log.
- Platforms such as ECS and Cloud Run can map a secret straight into an environment variable or a mounted file.

Secrets Manager's own docs make the point: you no longer need hard-coded credentials in application source code.

sections.heading: Rotation
sections.body:
A secret that never changes is a secret that eventually leaks. Plan for rotation from day one:

- **Managed rotation**: for many managed secrets, such as an RDS master password managed by Secrets Manager, the service configures and runs rotation itself.
- **Rotation by Lambda function**: for other secrets, Secrets Manager runs a function that updates both the secret and the database or service.
- Applications must tolerate rotation: read the secret at start-up and refresh it on authentication failure or on a schedule, rather than caching it forever.

Rotation is also your incident response. If a key leaks, you rotate it, rather than rebuilding and redeploying everything that embedded it.

sections.heading: Never bake secrets into images
sections.body:
Image layers are permanent and anyone who can pull the image can read them. Docker's docs warn that `ARG` and `ENV` "persist in the final image", so `ARG NPM_TOKEN` is a leak even if a later step deletes a file.

For secrets needed **during the build** (a private package registry token), use a BuildKit secret mount:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN npm ci
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN .
```

The secret is available only to that `RUN` step and is not written into a layer. Secrets needed **at runtime** come from the secret manager, never from the image.

keyPoints: Config varies per deploy and lives in the environment, not in code.
Build one image and promote it; inject config per environment at runtime.
Store secrets in a secret manager with IAM access control and audit logs.
Use managed or Lambda-based rotation and make apps tolerate rotation.
ARG and ENV persist in images; use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time secrets.

gotchas.trap: Pass a registry token as a build ARG and delete it in a later step.
gotchas.correct: ARG values persist in the image; use RUN --mount=type=secret.

gotchas.trap: Build a prod image and a staging image with different .env files baked in.
gotchas.correct: Build once and inject environment-specific config at deploy time.

gotchas.trap: Rotation means rebuilding the image with the new password.
gotchas.correct: Rotate in the secret manager; apps fetch the current value at runtime.

lessons.lab: Move a database password from a committed .env file into AWS Secrets Manager or Google Cloud Secret Manager, inject it into your container platform as an environment variable, and change a Dockerfile that used ARG for a registry token to use a BuildKit secret mount.
