questions.scenario: A team has three directories, dev, staging and prod, each with about 400 lines of nearly identical VPC and ECS configuration copied by hand. Last month a security group fix landed in prod but was never copied to staging.
questions.stem: What is the best way to restructure this so the environments stay consistent?
options: Manage staging and dev in the console and keep only prod in Terraform to reduce duplication.
Merge all three into one configuration and use count = 3 on every resource, indexing by environment.
Keep the copies but add a CI script that uses sed to sync changes from prod to the other directories.
Move the shared configuration into child modules with input variables, and keep a thin root configuration per environment that calls them with environment-specific values.
questions.explanation: Modules are Terraform's unit of reuse: shared logic lives once, and each environment root passes different variables. A fix in the module reaches every environment on its next plan. The other options either couple environments into one state, add fragile text tooling, or give up IaC entirely.
rationales: Console-managed environments drift and cannot be reviewed, defeating the purpose.
One configuration with count couples every environment into one state and one blast radius.
Text-syncing scripts are fragile and still duplicate the code.
Correct. Shared modules plus per-environment roots remove duplication while keeping separate state and variables.

questions.scenario: A root configuration calls module "db" which contains resource "aws_db_instance" "this". The root needs the database address to build a connection string for a service resource.
questions.stem: How should the root configuration get the address?
options: Reference module.db.aws_db_instance.this.address directly from the root module.
Read the address out of the state file with a local-exec provisioner.
Declare an output "address" in the db module and reference module.db.address from the root.
Hardcode the endpoint in a root locals block after the first apply.
questions.explanation: A calling module can only access values that a child module exposes through output blocks. Declaring an output and referencing module.db.address is the supported interface, and it keeps the dependency graph correct. Hardcoding or scraping state breaks when the database is replaced.
rationales: Child module resources are not directly addressable from the caller this way.
Scraping state with provisioners is brittle and bypasses the dependency graph.
Correct. Outputs are the interface a child module exposes to its caller.
A hardcoded value goes stale when the database is replaced and hides the dependency.

questions.scenario: A CI run and a developer laptop produced different plans for the same commit. Investigation shows CI downloaded a newer AWS provider release than the laptop had.
questions.stem: What change most directly prevents this?
options: Delete the .terraform directory before every run so providers are always fresh.
Commit .terraform.lock.hcl, which records the selected provider versions and checksums, and update it deliberately through reviewed changes.
Remove the version constraint from required_providers so Terraform always picks the same version.
Run terraform init -upgrade in CI on every run.
questions.explanation: The dependency lock file records the exact provider versions and checksums that terraform init selected. Committing it makes every machine use the same provider build, and the docs recommend reviewing changes to it like any other dependency change. Upgrading on every run does the opposite.
rationales: Deleting the cache forces re-download but, without a lock file, still picks whatever matches the constraint.
Correct. The committed lock file pins provider selections for every run.
No constraint makes selection less predictable, not more.
init -upgrade deliberately moves to newer versions, which is the cause of the mismatch.

questions.stem: A module input holds an API key. A developer marks the variable sensitive = true and concludes the key is now safe to keep in a widely readable state bucket. What is wrong with that conclusion?
options: Nothing; sensitive values are encrypted in state with a provider-managed key.
sensitive = true only applies to outputs, not variables.
Sensitive values are omitted from state but still appear in plan files.
sensitive = true only redacts the value in CLI output; it is still stored in plain text in state.
questions.explanation: Terraform still stores sensitive variable values in state; the flag only stops them from being shown in CLI output. Anyone who can read the state bucket can read the key. Restrict access to state, or keep the secret out of state with ephemeral values or write-only arguments.
rationales: Terraform does not encrypt sensitive values inside state.
Both variables and outputs can be marked sensitive.
Sensitive values are in both state and plan files; it is ephemeral values that are omitted.
Correct. Redaction applies only to CLI output.

sources.title: Sensitive data in state — Terraform docs

questions.scenario: A team is setting up a new S3 backend for Terraform state today and wants to prevent two CI jobs from applying at the same time.
questions.stem: Which backend configuration is the current recommended approach?
options: Create a DynamoDB table and set dynamodb_table in the backend block.
Set use_lockfile = true so the backend uses S3-native locking with a .tflock object.
Rely on S3 bucket versioning, which prevents concurrent writes.
Add -lock=false to CI commands and serialize jobs with a concurrency group instead.
questions.explanation: The S3 backend supports native locking through use_lockfile = true, which writes a .tflock object beside the state. DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated and slated for removal in a future minor version. Versioning helps recovery but does not lock.
rationales: DynamoDB locking still exists but is deprecated, so new setups should not depend on it.
Correct. S3-native locking is the supported mechanism going forward.
Versioning keeps old copies; it does not stop two writers.
Disabling Terraform locking removes protection against any run outside that one workflow.

questions.scenario: Terraform manages an RDS instance whose password comes from a variable marked sensitive = true. State lives in an S3 bucket with encrypt = true and no kms_key_id, so objects use S3-managed server-side encryption. A contractor has s3:GetObject on the whole bucket for an unrelated reporting job.
questions.stem: Which two statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: The contractor can read the database password in plain text from the state object.
Because encrypt = true is set, the state is unreadable to anyone except Terraform.
Tightening IAM on the state bucket, or keeping the password out of state (for example with write-only arguments or a service-managed password), addresses the exposure.
Moving the state file into the application's private Git repository would be a safer place for it.
questions.explanation: Terraform stores sensitive values in plain text in state, and S3 server-side encryption is transparent to anyone with read permission on the object. Restricting who can read state and keeping secrets out of state are the two real fixes. Committing state to Git spreads the secret to every clone.
rationales: Correct. sensitive only hides CLI output, and read access to the object returns plaintext.
encrypt = true is server-side encryption; authorized readers receive decrypted content.
Correct. Least-privilege access to state and keeping secrets out of it both reduce exposure.
Git history spreads the secret to every clone and keeps it forever.

sources.title: Sensitive data in state — Terraform docs

questions.scenario: During an incident an engineer added an inbound rule to a security group in the console. The team decides to keep the rule. The next terraform plan proposes removing it.
questions.stem: What is the best way to reconcile this?
options: Run terraform apply now; it will import the console change automatically.
Delete the state file and re-import every resource in the configuration.
Run terraform force-unlock to clear the drift marker.
Add the rule to the configuration, then confirm the next normal plan shows no changes; plan -refresh-only can be used to review and accept the drift into state first.
questions.explanation: A normal plan puts reality back to the configuration, so applying now would delete the rule. Refresh-only mode updates state to match remote changes without changing infrastructure, and updating the code makes the change permanent and reviewable. force-unlock only releases locks.
rationales: A normal apply would remove the console-added rule, not adopt it.
Rebuilding state from scratch is risky and unnecessary for one drifted attribute.
force-unlock releases a stuck state lock; there is no drift marker.
Correct. Codify the change and use refresh-only mode to reconcile state safely.

questions.scenario: An S3 bucket holding customer uploads was created by hand two years ago. The team wants Terraform to manage it from now on, with the change reviewed in a pull request like any other.
questions.stem: What approach fits best?
options: Edit the state JSON by hand to add the bucket entry.
Write a resource block with the same bucket name and run apply; Terraform adopts existing objects with matching names.
Delete the bucket, then let Terraform create a new one with the same name.
Add an import block with the bucket name as id, generate a starting resource block with plan -generate-config-out, and review the plan before applying.
questions.explanation: The import block brings an existing object under management through the normal plan and apply flow, so it can be reviewed. plan -generate-config-out drafts matching configuration to tidy up. Terraform does not adopt objects by name, and destroying a bucket of customer data is not an option.
rationales: Hand-editing state is error-prone and skips review.
Terraform tries to create a new bucket and fails because the name already exists.
Deleting the bucket destroys customer data.
Correct. Config-driven import is reviewable and keeps the real bucket.

questions.scenario: A GitHub Actions runner was cancelled mid-apply. Every new plan now fails with "Error acquiring the state lock" and prints a lock ID.
questions.stem: What should the on-call engineer do?
options: Delete the state object from S3 so the lock goes away.
Change every CI job to run with -lock=false.
Wait; Terraform state locks expire automatically after an hour.
Confirm no other plan or apply is still running, then run terraform force-unlock with that lock ID and re-run the pipeline.
questions.explanation: force-unlock exists for exactly this case: a lock left behind when automatic unlocking failed, identified by its lock ID. The docs warn that unlocking while someone else holds the lock allows multiple writers, so check first. Deleting state or disabling locking creates much bigger problems.
rationales: Deleting state loses the mapping to every managed resource.
Disabling locking permanently removes protection against concurrent writes.
You should not rely on a lock expiring by itself; force-unlock is the documented recovery.
Correct. Verify no active run, then release the specific lock by ID.

questions.scenario: A regulated team uses OpenTofu. Auditors want state to be unreadable even to an administrator who can download objects from the state bucket.
questions.stem: Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Set encrypt = true and a kms_key_id on the S3 backend.
Configure OpenTofu state encryption in a terraform { encryption { ... } } block with an aws_kms key provider and the aes_gcm method, set enforced = true, and protect the key.
Mark every secret variable sensitive = true.
Enable bucket versioning and object lock on the state bucket.
questions.explanation: OpenTofu can encrypt state client-side before it is written, so a reader of the bucket gets ciphertext. enforced = true prevents an unencrypted state from being written. Server-side S3 encryption is transparent to authorized readers, and losing the OpenTofu key means losing the state, so key protection matters.
rationales: S3 server-side encryption decrypts for anyone allowed to read the object.
Correct. Client-side state encryption is the OpenTofu feature that meets this requirement.
sensitive only redacts CLI output; state still holds plaintext.
Versioning and object lock protect against deletion, not reading.

questions.scenario: A shared VPC is being handed over to the platform team's separate configuration. The app team's configuration must stop managing it, but the VPC must keep running.
questions.stem: What should the app team change?
options: Delete the aws_vpc resource block and apply.
Add prevent_destroy = true to the VPC and then delete the resource block.
Add lifecycle { ignore_changes = all } to the VPC resource.
Replace the resource block with a removed block that sets lifecycle { destroy = false }, then apply.
questions.explanation: A removed block with destroy = false drops the resource from state while leaving the real object in place. Deleting the block plans a destroy, and prevent_destroy goes away with the block it lives in. ignore_changes keeps the resource managed, which is the opposite of the goal.
rationales: Removing the block makes Terraform plan to destroy the VPC.
prevent_destroy is removed together with the block, so it gives no protection here.
ignore_changes keeps the VPC in this state; the team still owns it.
Correct. removed with destroy = false forgets the resource without deleting it.

questions.scenario: A team posts terraform plan output on pull requests. After merge, the pipeline runs terraform apply -auto-approve, which plans again. Once, a teammate's concurrent change meant the applied plan differed from what was reviewed.
questions.stem: Which change best guarantees that what was approved is what gets applied?
options: Increase the lock timeout so applies wait longer.
Add -refresh=false to the apply so it reuses the reviewed state.
Have the reviewer run terraform apply from their laptop after approving.
After merge, run terraform plan -out=tfplan, require approval on a protected environment, then run terraform apply tfplan.
questions.explanation: Applying a saved plan file executes exactly the reviewed actions, and Terraform rejects the plan if state changed since it was created. An environment approval gate puts a human check between plan and apply. Saved plans contain plaintext values, so store the artifact securely.
rationales: Lock timeouts serialize runs but do not make the applied plan match the reviewed one.
Skipping refresh hides drift and still re-plans.
Laptop applies bypass CI controls and audit.
Correct. A saved plan plus an approval gate makes review and apply match.

questions.scenario: A startup uses one Terraform configuration with CLI workspaces named staging and prod in the same S3 backend, and the same CI role applies both. A security review asks that staging credentials must never be able to change prod.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Keep workspaces and add terraform.workspace conditionals that skip prod resources when in staging.
Create a third workspace for production hotfixes.
Encrypt the prod workspace state with a different KMS key while keeping the same role.
Split into separate root configurations per environment, each with its own backend and CI role, ideally in separate cloud accounts, sharing code through modules.
questions.explanation: Workspaces store multiple states in the same backend, and the Terraform docs say they are not a suitable isolation mechanism when environments need separate credentials. Separate configurations and backends, with separate roles and accounts, make the boundary real. Conditionals and extra workspaces leave the shared role in place.
rationales: Conditionals do not change who can access prod state or resources.
Another workspace adds a third environment to the same shared backend.
The same role can still use the key, so the boundary is unchanged.
Correct. Separate backends, roles and accounts give real isolation.

questions.scenario: The prod RDS resource has lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }. The team is reviewing what this setting does and does not protect against.
questions.stem: Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: A plan that would destroy or replace the database fails with an error.
It also blocks someone from deleting the database in the AWS console.
If a pull request deletes the whole resource block, prevent_destroy no longer applies and the plan shows a destroy.
It can be set to var.is_prod so only the prod environment is protected.
questions.explanation: prevent_destroy causes Terraform to reject any plan that would destroy the resource, including a forced replacement. It lives in the resource block, so deleting the block removes the protection. It has no effect outside Terraform, and lifecycle arguments accept literal values only.
rationales: Correct. Any planned destroy of the resource is an error.
It is a Terraform setting and does nothing to console or API deletions; use deletion protection for that.
Correct. The protection goes away with the block it is declared in.
Lifecycle arguments must be literal values, not variables.

questions.scenario: Changing the domain on an ACM certificate forces Terraform to replace it. By default the plan destroys the old certificate first, and the load balancer listener that uses it would break in between.
questions.stem: Which lifecycle setting addresses this?
options: ignore_changes = [domain_name]
create_before_destroy = true
prevent_destroy = true
replace_triggered_by = [aws_lb.main]
questions.explanation: create_before_destroy makes Terraform create the replacement first, update dependents, and only then destroy the old object. ignore_changes would silently skip the domain change, and prevent_destroy would make the plan fail. replace_triggered_by forces more replacements, not fewer gaps.
rationales: Ignoring the attribute means the domain change never happens.
Correct. The new certificate exists before the old one is removed.
prevent_destroy blocks the required replacement with an error.
This triggers replacement when the load balancer changes, which is unrelated.

questions.scenario: A GitHub Actions workflow applies Terraform to prod using an IAM user's access key stored as a repository secret. The key has not been rotated in two years.
questions.stem: What is the recommended replacement?
options: Rotate the access key every 90 days with a scheduled workflow.
Move the access key from a repository secret to an organization secret.
Commit an encrypted credentials file and decrypt it in the workflow.
Grant the job id-token: write and assume an IAM role through OIDC, with the role trust policy limited to the repository's prod environment sub claim, and require reviewers on that environment.
questions.explanation: OIDC lets the workflow exchange a short-lived token for temporary role credentials, so no long-lived key exists to leak. Restricting the trust policy to the environment sub claim, with required reviewers on that environment, means the prod role is usable only after approval. The other options keep a long-lived secret. For repositories created after 2026-07-15 the sub claim uses an immutable ID-based format, so write the trust condition to match the claim the repository actually emits.
rationales: Rotation reduces but does not remove the risk of a long-lived key.
Changing the secret scope widens access rather than removing the key.
An encrypted file is still a long-lived credential plus a decryption key to manage.
Correct. Short-lived OIDC credentials scoped to an approved environment.

sources.title: OIDC in AWS — GitHub Actions docs
Deployments and environments — GitHub Actions docs

questions.scenario: A refactor moves aws_s3_bucket.assets into a new module, so its address becomes module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.assets. The prod plan now shows 1 to add and 1 to destroy for that bucket.
questions.stem: What should the author do before merging?
options: Merge anyway; Terraform recreates the bucket and copies its objects.
Add a moved block from aws_s3_bucket.assets to module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.assets and confirm the plan shows no destroy.
Add prevent_destroy to the bucket so the destroy is skipped and the add still happens.
Run terraform apply -target on the new address only.
questions.explanation: A moved block tells Terraform that the resource changed address, so it updates state instead of destroying and creating. The reviewer should see the plan change to a move with no destroy. Terraform does not copy bucket contents, and prevent_destroy would simply make the plan fail.
rationales: Terraform would destroy the old bucket and create an empty one; it does not copy data.
Correct. moved records the new address and avoids the replace.
prevent_destroy causes the plan to error, not a partial apply.
Targeting the new address creates a second bucket and leaves the destroy pending.

questions.scenario: A five-person startup runs dev, staging and prod in one AWS account, separated by tags and VPCs. A developer with broad dev permissions accidentally deleted a prod S3 object.
questions.stem: What is the most effective structural fix?
options: Move prod into its own VPC in the same account.
Add an Environment tag to every resource and train developers to check it.
Create one IAM user per developer per environment in the same account.
Use separate AWS accounts per environment under AWS Organizations, with SCP guardrails, and give people federated, temporary access per account.
questions.explanation: The account is the strongest isolation boundary on AWS, and the IAM best practices recommend multiple accounts under Organizations with SCPs as guardrails. Federated access with temporary credentials then controls who can reach each account. Tags and VPCs do not stop IAM permissions from spanning environments.
rationales: VPCs isolate networks, not IAM permissions on services like S3.
Tags help organize but do not enforce isolation by themselves.
Many IAM users with long-lived keys work against the best practices.
Correct. Separate accounts isolate permissions, billing and blast radius.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM — AWS IAM User Guide
Organizing your AWS environment — AWS Whitepaper

questions.scenario: A platform engineer is designing guardrails for an AWS Organization with separate prod and dev accounts, and lets developers create IAM roles for their own Lambda functions in dev.
questions.stem: Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: An SCP that allows s3:* gives every principal in the account S3 access.
SCPs do not grant permissions; principals still need IAM policies that allow the action.
A permissions boundary on developer-created roles caps the maximum permissions those roles can have.
IAM Access Analyzer issues temporary credentials to roles that need extra permissions.
questions.explanation: SCPs and RCPs are guardrails that limit what is possible in an account; they grant nothing by themselves. Permissions boundaries are how you delegate role creation safely, because a role can never exceed its boundary. Access Analyzer generates and validates policies; it does not issue credentials.
rationales: An allow in an SCP only permits the action to be granted; it grants nothing.
Correct. Effective access needs both the guardrail and an identity or resource policy.
Correct. Boundaries cap what delegated roles can do.
Access Analyzer analyzes, generates and validates policies; it does not issue credentials.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM — AWS IAM User Guide
Service control policies — AWS Organizations User Guide

questions.scenario: An app runs in ECS tasks in private subnets with security group sg-app. A Postgres RDS instance needs to accept connections only from those tasks, whose IP addresses change on every deploy.
questions.stem: How should the database security group be configured?
options: Allow inbound 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0 and rely on the database password.
Allow inbound 5432 from the VPC CIDR and add a deny rule for the public subnets.
Put the database in a public subnet and allow only the office IP.
Allow inbound 5432 with sg-app as the source, and keep the database in private subnets.
questions.explanation: A security group rule can name another security group as its source, so access follows the app tasks as their IPs change. Security groups support allow rules only, so a deny rule is not possible. Keeping the database in private subnets removes any direct internet path.
rationales: Opening the port to the internet exposes the database to scanning and brute force.
Security groups have no deny rules, and the whole VPC is broader than needed.
A public subnet adds an internet path and does not cover the app tasks.
Correct. Security group referencing plus private subnets gives least-privilege network access.

sources.title: Security group rules — Amazon VPC User Guide
Subnets for your VPC — Amazon VPC User Guide

questions.scenario: Private-subnet tasks read and write large volumes of data to S3 in the same Region. The monthly bill shows high NAT gateway data processing charges.
questions.stem: What is the most cost-effective fix?
options: Add a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and associate it with the private subnets' route tables.
Move the tasks to public subnets and give each a public IPv4 address.
Add a second NAT gateway in another Availability Zone.
Compress the objects before upload and keep routing through the NAT gateway.
questions.explanation: A gateway endpoint for S3 routes that traffic privately from the VPC and has no additional charge, so it stops passing through the NAT gateway, which bills per GB processed. Public IPv4 addresses are billed hourly and widen exposure. More NAT gateways add cost.
rationales: Correct. S3 gateway endpoints bypass the NAT gateway at no additional charge.
Public IPv4 addresses cost money even when idle and expose the tasks.
Another NAT gateway adds hourly and per-GB charges.
Compression reduces the volume somewhat but keeps paying NAT processing for every byte.

sources.title: Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 — AWS PrivateLink Guide

questions.scenario: A team's prod Postgres runs on a single RDS instance. They want automatic failover if the instance's Availability Zone fails, with minimal operational work.
questions.stem: What should they enable?
options: A nightly snapshot copied to another Region.
A Multi-AZ deployment, which keeps a standby DB instance in another Availability Zone for automatic failover.
A read replica in the same Availability Zone.
Migrate to self-managed Postgres on two EC2 instances with a custom failover script.
questions.explanation: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment maintains a standby in a different Availability Zone and fails over to it. Snapshots are for recovery from data loss, not fast failover. A same-AZ replica fails with the zone, and self-managed failover adds the work the team wants to avoid.
rationales: Snapshots help disaster recovery but mean a slow manual restore, not failover.
Correct. Multi-AZ provides a standby in another AZ for failover.
A replica in the same AZ shares the failure domain.
Self-managed failover is exactly the operational burden a managed database removes.

sources.title: Multi-AZ deployments — Amazon RDS User Guide

questions.stem: Developers on a small team need console and CLI access to the company AWS accounts. Which approach follows IAM best practices?
options: One shared IAM user per account whose access key is kept in the team password manager.
An IAM user per developer with access keys rotated every 90 days.
Root user credentials for admins and IAM users for everyone else.
Federated access through IAM Identity Center with temporary credentials and phishing-resistant MFA.
questions.explanation: AWS recommends that humans use federation with an identity provider to get temporary credentials, and that MFA is required, preferably phishing-resistant. Long-lived access keys and shared users go against the guidance, and the root user should not be used for daily work.
rationales: Shared users remove accountability and keep long-lived keys around.
Rotation helps, but long-lived per-user keys are still discouraged for people.
The root user is not for routine administration.
Correct. Federation plus temporary credentials and strong MFA.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM — AWS IAM User Guide

questions.scenario: A team builds two images per release, app:staging and app:prod, each with a different .env file copied in. A bug appeared in prod that staging never showed, because the images differed.
questions.stem: Which practice best fixes this?
options: Add a CI check that diffs the two .env files before building.
Build one image per commit and inject environment-specific config, such as database URLs, at deploy time through environment variables and a secret manager.
Build only the prod image and test it directly in prod with feature flags.
Move config into a constants file in the codebase so it is versioned.
questions.explanation: Twelve-factor config says config varies per deploy and belongs in the environment, strictly separated from code. Building once and injecting config at runtime means the image tested in staging is the image that runs in prod. Constants in code are the anti-pattern the factor warns against.
rationales: Diffing files does not remove the different artifacts.
Correct. One artifact, with config supplied by each environment.
Skipping staging removes the safety net rather than fixing the build.
Config in code violates strict separation of config from code.

questions.scenario: A Dockerfile has ARG NPM_TOKEN, writes it to .npmrc, runs npm ci, and then deletes .npmrc in a later RUN step. The image is pushed to a registry that the whole engineering org can pull from.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Delete .npmrc in the same RUN step as npm ci.
Switch from ARG to ENV so the token is only available at runtime.
Squash the image layers before pushing.
Use RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN npm ci and pass the token with docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN, then revoke the leaked token.
questions.explanation: Docker's docs warn that build arguments and environment variables persist in the final image, so the token is exposed regardless of later deletions. A BuildKit secret mount exposes the token only to that RUN step without writing it to a layer. Because the token already shipped, it must be revoked.
rationales: The ARG value is still recorded in the image metadata.
ENV also persists in the final image, which is worse.
Squashing does not undo a token that has already shipped or that sits in metadata.
Correct. Secret mounts keep build-time secrets out of image layers and metadata, and the exposed token needs revoking.

questions.scenario: A team wants its prod RDS master password to rotate regularly without code changes or redeploys, and wants nobody to have to handle the password by hand.
questions.stem: Which two practices together meet this goal? (Select two.)
options: Let RDS manage the master user password in AWS Secrets Manager, which handles rotation.
Have the application read the credentials from Secrets Manager at runtime and refresh them on authentication failure, rather than baking them into the image.
Keep the password in a terraform.tfvars file in the repo and change it each quarter.
Rebuild and redeploy the container image with the new password each time it rotates.
questions.explanation: RDS integrates with Secrets Manager to manage master user passwords, and managed rotation needs no custom function. Applications that fetch the secret at runtime pick up the new value after rotation. Passwords in tfvars or images are hard-coded credentials that rotation cannot reach.
rationales: Correct. The service generates, stores and rotates the password.
Correct. Runtime retrieval lets apps follow rotation without redeploys.
tfvars in a repo puts the secret in Git history and state, and needs manual handling.
Baking secrets into images leaks them and ties rotation to deploys.

sources.title: Password management with Secrets Manager — Amazon RDS User Guide
Rotate secrets — AWS Secrets Manager User Guide

questions.scenario: A Terraform 1.17 configuration sets an API key on a resource argument. Security wants the key to appear in neither the state file nor saved plan files.
questions.stem: Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Mark the variable sensitive = true.
Expose the key as a sensitive output so it is tracked separately.
Store the key in terraform.tfvars and add that file to .gitignore.
Supply the key through an ephemeral value to a write-only argument (a *_wo argument, with *_wo_version to trigger updates), which Terraform does not store in state or plan.
questions.explanation: Ephemeral values are omitted from state and plan files, and write-only arguments, available from Terraform 1.11, accept such values without persisting them. sensitive only redacts output, and both outputs and tfvars still put the value into state. The version argument tells Terraform when to send a new value.
rationales: sensitive values are still written to state and plan.
Outputs are stored in state, so this adds another copy.
The value still ends up in state once applied to the resource.
Correct. Ephemeral values with write-only arguments are kept out of state and plan.

sources.title: Sensitive data in state — Terraform docs

questions.scenario: A service on Google Cloud reads a third-party API key from a constant in its source code. The repository is about to be shared with an outside contractor.
questions.stem: What is the best first step?
options: Rotate the key, store the new one in Secret Manager, grant the service account access to that secret, and inject it into the service at runtime.
Move the key to a config.yaml file in the same repository.
Base64-encode the key in the source so it is not readable at a glance.
Make the repository private again and keep the key in code.
questions.explanation: A secret manager stores the secret with per-secret access control and audit, and the service reads it at runtime so it never lives in code. Because the key has been in source history, it must be rotated. Encoding or moving the key to another file in the repo still leaks it.
rationales: Correct. Rotate the exposed key and serve the new one from Secret Manager.
A config file in the repo is still committed to history.
Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.
The key remains in history for everyone with access, now and later.

sources.title: Secret Manager overview — Google Cloud docs

questions.scenario: A four-person team runs a Node.js API and a worker that consumes from a queue. Traces from the API stop at the publish call, and the worker’s spans appear as separate traces with no parent.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: The Collector is using head sampling instead of tail sampling.
The worker’s logs are not structured as JSON.
The API and worker export to different Collector ports.
Trace context is not being propagated through the queue messages to the worker.
questions.explanation: Spans from different processes join one trace only when the caller passes trace context to the callee. Queue hops are a common place where context is dropped unless it is injected into message headers and extracted on consume. Sampling, log format and export ports do not create orphaned parentless traces.
rationales: Sampling decides which traces are kept; it does not split one trace into unrelated ones.
Log format affects log search, not the parent-child links between spans.
Exporting to different ports of the same Collector still preserves trace IDs if context was propagated.
Correct: without propagated context the worker starts a new root trace for each message.

questions.scenario: A developer adds an otlp receiver and an exporter to the top of an OpenTelemetry Collector config and deploys it in a container. Apps in other containers get connection refused on port 4318.
questions.stem: Which two changes together fix the problem? (Select two.)
options: Switch the apps from OTLP over HTTP to Prometheus scraping.
Bind the receiver endpoints to 0.0.0.0 instead of the default localhost.
Add the receiver and exporter to a pipeline under service.pipelines.
Put the batch processor before the receiver in the config file.
questions.explanation: A Collector component only runs if it is listed in service.pipelines, so a receiver defined only at the top level never starts. Receivers also default to localhost, which other containers cannot reach, so they must bind 0.0.0.0:4317 and 0.0.0.0:4318.
rationales: Changing protocols avoids rather than fixes the misconfiguration, and the apps already speak OTLP.
Correct: the localhost default rejects connections from other containers.
Correct: components not referenced in a pipeline are not started.
Processors sit between receivers and exporters within a pipeline; file position does not start a receiver.

questions.scenario: Your API dashboard shows the server span error ratio climbing whenever a mobile client bug sends requests for non-existent order IDs. The server returns 404 and the team wants to keep paging on server span errors.
questions.stem: According to OpenTelemetry HTTP semantic conventions, how should these server spans be recorded?
options: Leave the server span status unset for the 404; the client span records it as Error.
Set the server span status to Error for any status code of 400 or above.
Set the server span status to Ok explicitly for every 4xx response.
Drop the spans for 4xx responses at the Collector.
questions.explanation: HTTP semconv says a server leaves span status unset for 4xx responses, since the request was the client’s fault, while the client span marks 4xx as Error. Only 5xx is an Error on the server side. Instrumentation that marks every 4xx as a server Error inflates server error rates exactly as described.
rationales: Correct: 4xx is unset on the server span and Error on the client span.
This is the anti-pattern that makes client bugs look like server failures.
The convention is to leave status unset, not to set Ok on 4xx.
Dropping spans loses useful data; the fix is correct status, not deletion.

questions.stem: A team names HTTP server spans after the raw request path, such as GET /orders/8812. Their tracing backend becomes slow and expensive. What should the span name be instead?
options: A random UUID per request so names never collide.
Only the HTTP method, such as GET.
The method and route template, such as GET /orders/{id}.
The full URL including query string, for exact matching.
questions.explanation: OTel HTTP semantic conventions name server spans {method} {http.route} and say they must not fall back to the raw path. The route template keeps span names low-cardinality while still identifying the endpoint. The concrete path belongs in an attribute such as url.path.
rationales: Unique names destroy any ability to aggregate by endpoint.
Method alone is low-cardinality but cannot tell endpoints apart.
Correct: the route template bounds cardinality and is what semconv specifies.
Full URLs make cardinality even worse and can leak data in query strings.

questions.scenario: A small team wants to keep tracing costs down but has lost the traces for several rare checkout failures because they were not sampled.
questions.stem: Which sampling approach best keeps failing and slow traces, and what is its trade-off?
options: Head sampling at a higher rate, which keeps every error at no extra cost.
Tail sampling, which sees the full trace before deciding but is stateful and costlier to run.
Turning off sampling on the client so the server decides at the first span.
Head sampling at 100% in production, which has no cost impact for a small team.
questions.explanation: Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete, so it can keep errors and slow traces specifically. The OpenTelemetry sampling docs note it is stateful and more costly to operate. Head sampling decides early and cheaply but cannot know whether a trace will fail.
rationales: A higher head rate keeps more traces at random, still not every error, and costs more.
Correct: tail sampling can select on outcome, at the cost of buffering whole traces.
Deciding at the first server span is still head sampling and is still blind to outcome.
Keeping 100% is the cost problem the team is trying to avoid.

questions.scenario: A Python service team plans to rip out its logging library and emit logs only through the OpenTelemetry Python logs SDK, because "OTel logs are stable now".
questions.stem: What is the best advice?
options: Proceed; every OTel signal is stable in every language.
Avoid OpenTelemetry for logs entirely because the logs spec is experimental.
Send logs as span events only, since traces are the only stable signal.
Check the OTel status page: the logs spec is stable but the Python logs SDK is still in development, so bridge the existing library rather than depending on it alone.
questions.explanation: The specification status lists the logs SDK spec as stable, but per-language status shows the Python and JS logs SDKs still in development. Keeping a mature logging library and bridging it lowers the risk. Metrics and traces are stable in Python, so traces are not the only stable signal.
rationales: Language SDKs lag the spec; not every signal is stable everywhere.
The logs spec (Bridge API and SDK) is stable, so this overcorrects.
Metrics are also stable in Python, and abusing span events loses log semantics.
Correct: stability differs per language and must be checked.

questions.scenario: An on-call engineer at a startup is paged four times a night for "CPU above 85%" on one of three API replicas. Latency and error rates stay normal each time.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Route the CPU page to a shared channel that everyone watches at night.
Remove the CPU page, show CPU on a dashboard or ticket, and page on user-visible symptoms such as SLO burn rate.
Raise the CPU threshold to 95% so it pages less often.
Add a fourth replica and keep the CPU page as it is.
questions.explanation: High CPU here is a cause with no user-visible symptom, and the SRE book says to page on symptoms and require every page to be urgent and actionable. Moving it to a dashboard or ticket keeps the information without waking anyone. Tuning the threshold or the channel still pages on a cause.
rationales: Spreading the noise to more people does not make it actionable.
Correct: page on symptoms; causes belong on dashboards and tickets.
A higher threshold still pages on a cause that users do not feel.
More capacity may lower CPU but the alert remains a non-actionable cause page.

questions.stem: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. For the last hour its error ratio has been 1.44%, and the last 5 minutes are similar. What does the SRE Workbook recommend?
options: Page only if the 3-day window also shows a burn rate above 1.
Do nothing until 100% of the error budget is consumed.
Open a ticket: a 1.44% error ratio is well within normal variance.
Page: this is a 14.4x burn rate, consuming about 2% of the monthly budget per hour.
questions.explanation: Burn rate is the error rate divided by 1 minus the SLO, so 0.0144 / 0.001 = 14.4. The Workbook’s table pages at 14.4x over a 1 h long window and 5 m short window, which corresponds to 2% of a 30-day budget. At that rate the whole budget would be gone in about 50 hours.
rationales: The 3-day window is the ticket tier; it is not a precondition for the fast-burn page.
Waiting for the full budget to be gone defeats the purpose of alerting.
A ticket is for the slow 1x burn over 3 days, not 14.4x.
Correct: 14.4x over 1 h and 5 m is the first paging tier.

questions.scenario: A team alerts on SLO burn using only a 1-hour window. After a bad deploy is rolled back, the alert keeps firing for almost an hour, and people start silencing it.
questions.stem: What change does the SRE Workbook recommend?
options: Lengthen the window to 6 hours so the alert is more stable.
Replace the burn-rate alert with a static error-count threshold.
Add an automatic 60-minute silence after every firing.
Require a short window (such as 5 minutes) to also exceed the threshold, combined with "and", so the alert resets quickly.
questions.explanation: The Workbook’s multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts pair a long window with a short one, both above threshold. The long window prevents paging on brief blips, and the short window makes the alert stop soon after the problem is fixed. A longer single window makes the reset delay worse.
rationales: A longer single window resets even more slowly.
Static counts ignore traffic volume and the SLO, and still have the reset issue.
Blanket silences hide a real recurrence.
Correct: the short window gives fast reset while the long window filters noise.

questions.stem: A two-engineer SaaS team is choosing an availability SLO. Which statement about a 99.9% SLO over 30 days is accurate?
options: It allows about 7 hours of full downtime in the window.
It allows no downtime; any outage breaches it.
It allows about 43 minutes of full downtime in the window.
It allows about 4 minutes of full downtime in the window.
questions.explanation: The error budget is 1 minus the SLO, here 0.1% of 30 days, which is 43.2 minutes. About 4.3 minutes corresponds to 99.99%, and 432 minutes (about 7 hours) to 99%. An SLO below 100% always leaves some budget.
rationales: About 7.2 hours is the 99% budget.
Any SLO below 100% has a non-zero budget.
Correct: 0.001 x 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes.
About 4.3 minutes is the 99.99% budget.

questions.scenario: A team’s only alert is an error-rate threshold computed from application logs. One evening their TLS certificate expires and customers cannot connect, but no alert fires for two hours.
questions.stem: What would most directly have caught this?
options: Adding CPU and memory alerts on the application hosts.
Lowering the application error-rate threshold.
An external uptime or synthetic check that connects over HTTPS from outside, from multiple locations.
Sampling 100% of traces.
questions.explanation: When TLS fails, requests never reach the application, so app logs, metrics and traces show nothing wrong. An external probe connecting the way a user does fails immediately. Running it from several locations avoids paging on a single probe’s network glitch.
rationales: Host resources look normal, or even lower, when traffic stops.
There are no app errors to count, so any threshold stays quiet.
Correct: only an outside-in check sees failures before traffic reaches the app.
No requests arrive, so there are no traces to sample.

questions.scenario: You are designing synthetic monitoring for a checkout flow with a small budget and a team that already struggles with alert fatigue.
questions.stem: Which practices should you adopt? (Select two.)
options: Run the scripted journey from more than one location and alert only when several locations fail.
Use a dedicated test account and keep the journey idempotent or clean up after it.
Check only a /ping endpoint that returns 200 without touching dependencies, to avoid false alarms.
Page on every single failed probe run so no outage is missed.
questions.explanation: Requiring failures from several locations filters probe-side network blips, which keeps pages actionable. A dedicated, idempotent test account stops synthetic traffic from polluting real data. A trivial /ping misses dependency failures, and paging on each failed run is a classic noisy-alert anti-pattern.
rationales: Correct: multi-location confirmation reduces false pages.
Correct: isolated, repeatable journeys are safe to run on a schedule.
A ping that ignores dependencies can stay green while checkout is broken.
Single-run paging creates exactly the alert fatigue the team wants to avoid.

questions.scenario: After each deploy, a team searches thousands of raw exception log lines to decide whether the release made things worse.
questions.stem: Which approach gives the clearest release-health signal?
options: Increase log verbosity to DEBUG for a day after each release.
Compare this week’s total exception count with last week’s.
Group exceptions into issues tagged with the release version, and review new issues and regressions per release.
Page on-call for every exception logged after a deploy.
questions.explanation: Grouping identical exceptions and tagging each with the release turns thousands of lines into a short list of new or regressed issues tied to a specific version. That lets the team decide quickly whether to roll back. Paging on every exception is noisy, and week-over-week totals mix many releases and traffic changes.
rationales: More logs make the search problem worse, not better.
Weekly totals cannot attribute a change to a specific release.
Correct: release-tagged, grouped issues show what this release changed.
Paging per exception overwhelms on-call with non-actionable noise.

questions.scenario: A team canaries each release to 5% of traffic in the late afternoon and compares the canary’s error rate with the whole service’s error rate from the previous morning.
questions.stem: What is the main flaw, according to SRE canarying guidance?
options: The comparison should be against a control population running the old version over the same time window.
The canary should run for a full week before any comparison.
Canary analysis should only use CPU and memory, not error rates.
Canaries should receive at least 50% of traffic to be statistically meaningful.
questions.explanation: Traffic mix and load change across the day, so comparing a canary to a different time period confounds the release with time effects. The SRE Workbook compares the canary with a control population on the same metrics at the same time. A small canary percentage is the point, not a flaw.
rationales: Correct: canary and control must be compared over the same window.
A week-long canary slows delivery and still needs a same-time control.
User-facing metrics such as error rate are central to canary evaluation.
A small canary limits blast radius; 50% defeats the purpose.

questions.scenario: Fifteen minutes after a deploy, checkout error rates jump. The on-call engineer suspects a specific code change and wants to attach a debugger in production to confirm it before acting.
questions.stem: What should happen first?
options: Wait for the next scheduled deploy to ship a fix forward.
Capture key evidence such as the build ID and logs, then roll back to restore service and investigate afterwards.
Keep debugging in production until the exact root cause is proven.
Write the postmortem draft while the issue is fresh, then roll back.
questions.explanation: The SRE book’s incident priorities are to stop the bleeding, restore service and preserve evidence. Noting the build ID and saving logs takes moments and does not delay mitigation, and a rollback is a fast, low-risk fix when an incident lines up with a deploy. Root-cause analysis and the postmortem come after users are no longer affected.
rationales: Waiting for a later deploy leaves users broken in the meantime.
Correct: preserve what you need, then mitigate before diagnosing.
Debugging live prolongs user impact for a cause you can study later.
The postmortem is written after the incident, not during it.

questions.scenario: An engineer has been looking at intermittent login failures for 70 minutes. A few customers have emailed support, and the issue may involve the identity provider team.
questions.stem: Based on SRE incident guidance, what should the engineer do?
options: Keep investigating alone until a root cause is confirmed, then decide whether it was an incident.
Declare an incident only if the issue becomes a full outage.
Open a low-priority ticket for the identity team and log off.
Declare an incident now: it is customer-visible, may need a second team, and has been unsolved for over an hour.
questions.explanation: The SRE book suggests declaring if any one of three conditions holds: a second team is needed, the issue is visible to customers, or it is unsolved after an hour of focused analysis. All three apply here. Declaring early is cheap and gives the response a commander and a clear structure.
rationales: Waiting for a root cause delays coordination and communication.
Partial, customer-visible failures already meet the criteria.
A ticket ignores ongoing customer impact.
Correct: any one trigger is enough, and all three are met.

questions.scenario: During a SEV1, three engineers are each restarting services and changing config at the same time, the CEO is asking each of them for status in chat, and nobody is sure who is in charge.
questions.stem: Which actions best fix the response? (Select three.)
options: Let each engineer continue their own fix to maximise parallel effort.
Assign a communications lead to post updates on a fixed cadence to stakeholders.
Have one operations lead be the only person changing production.
Name an explicit incident commander who coordinates and assigns work.
questions.explanation: The SRE book’s incident roles separate coordination (incident commander), changes to the system (operations lead) and stakeholder updates (communications lead). This stops conflicting changes and shields the people fixing the system from status requests. Uncoordinated parallel changes are the freelancing anti-pattern the roles exist to prevent.
rationales: Uncoordinated parallel changes make the incident harder to understand and fix.
Correct: a communications lead handles updates so responders can focus.
Correct: a single operations lead avoids conflicting changes.
Correct: an explicit IC coordinates and decides.

questions.scenario: A junior engineer ran a migration script against production that deleted a table’s recent rows. The team restored from backup within an hour. A manager wants the postmortem to record the engineer’s name and a warning to be more careful.
questions.stem: What is the best approach to the postmortem?
options: Record the engineer’s name and require them to sign off on future migrations.
Publish a short note that says "be more careful with migrations" and close it.
Write a blameless postmortem on how the system allowed the script to run against production, with specific, owned action items such as guardrails and review.
Skip the postmortem because the data was restored within an hour.
questions.explanation: Any data loss is a postmortem trigger in the SRE book, even if it was restored. Blameless postmortems focus on the system conditions that allowed the mistake, because blame makes people hide information. Action items should be specific, owned and tracked, not exhortations.
rationales: Naming and punishing discourages honest reporting and does not fix the system.
"Be more careful" is not an actionable, trackable item.
Correct: blameless review with concrete, owned fixes.
Data loss triggers a postmortem regardless of how fast it was restored.

questions.scenario: A customer emailed to report that file uploads had been failing for six hours. No alert fired. An engineer fixed a misconfigured bucket policy in ten minutes, and the team wants to move on.
questions.stem: Why does this warrant a postmortem, and what should it focus on?
options: It warrants one only if more than one customer complained.
It is a monitoring failure, since the issue was found manually; the review should cover why no alert or check detected it, along with the fix.
It does not warrant one, because the fix took only ten minutes.
It warrants one only to identify who changed the bucket policy.
questions.explanation: The SRE book lists a monitoring failure, meaning an issue discovered manually rather than by alerting, as a postmortem trigger. The six-hour detection gap matters more than the ten-minute fix, so action items should add detection such as an upload SLI or a synthetic upload check. Blame-oriented or threshold-on-complaints reasoning misses the lesson.
rationales: User-visible impact and the monitoring failure already qualify it.
Correct: the detection gap is itself a trigger and the key lesson.
Time to fix is not the issue; six hours undetected is.
Postmortems are blameless and focus on the system.

questions.scenario: A five-person team’s on-call rotation has grown to 30 pages a week, most auto-resolving within minutes, and two engineers have asked to leave the rotation.
questions.stem: What is the most effective first step?
options: Add a third person to each shift so the load is spread more thinly.
Review every page against "urgent, actionable, needs human judgment", then delete, automate or downgrade the ones that fail and add runbooks to the rest.
Mute alerts overnight and review them each morning.
Increase the alert evaluation interval so fewer alerts fire.
questions.explanation: Most of these pages are not actionable, since they resolve on their own, which fails the SRE book’s test for a page. Removing, automating or ticketing them fixes the cause of burnout, and runbooks make the remaining pages faster to handle. Spreading or muting the noise leaves the underlying problem and can hide real incidents.
rationales: More people share the noise but do not reduce it.
Correct: fix the alerts themselves so each page deserves a human.
Blanket overnight muting risks missing a real SEV1.
Slower evaluation delays real alerts as well as noisy ones.

questions.scenario: Order database
questions.stem: The business owner of an order system says: "We can lose at most 5 minutes of orders, and the shop must be taking orders again within 4 hours of an outage." Which statement correctly expresses these requirements?
options: RTO is 5 minutes and RPO is 4 hours
Both targets are met by a nightly snapshot copied to another Region
MTTR must be under 4 hours and RPO is not needed because backups run nightly
RPO is 5 minutes and RTO is 4 hours
questions.explanation: RPO is the maximum acceptable time since the last recovery point, so it bounds data loss (5 minutes). RTO is the maximum acceptable delay before service is restored (4 hours). A nightly snapshot could lose up to 24 hours of data.
rationales: This swaps the definitions: data loss is RPO, downtime is RTO.
A nightly snapshot allows up to a day of data loss, far beyond a 5-minute RPO.
MTTR is an average across incidents, not a per-event target, and a data-loss bound is explicitly required.
Correct. Data loss maps to RPO and downtime maps to RTO.

sources.title: Disaster recovery objectives — AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

questions.scenario: Accidental delete
questions.stem: At 14:02 a migration script ran `DELETE FROM invoices` without a WHERE clause on a production Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance. Automated backups are enabled, and the instance is Multi-AZ with one read replica. What is the best way to recover the data?
options: Restore the instance to a point just before 14:02, which creates a new DB instance, verify it, then copy the rows back or repoint the application
Force a Multi-AZ failover so the standby takes over with the original data
Promote the read replica, since it still holds the deleted rows
Restore the instance in place to 14:01 so the endpoint does not change
questions.explanation: Point-in-time recovery restores to a moment before the mistake, and on RDS it always creates a new DB instance. The replica and the Multi-AZ standby both applied the DELETE within seconds, so neither holds the old data. After verifying the restored instance, you either copy the affected rows back or switch the app to it.
rationales: Correct. PITR to a new instance is the documented recovery path for logical mistakes.
The synchronous standby applied the DELETE too; failover just moves the problem.
The read replica replicated the DELETE and no longer has the rows.
RDS point-in-time restore does not rewind an existing instance in place.

sources.title: Restoring a DB instance to a specified time — Amazon RDS User Guide
Disaster recovery options in the cloud — AWS Whitepapers

questions.scenario: Replication instead of backups
questions.stem: A team replicates its production database continuously to a second Region and proposes to turn off scheduled backups to save money. They also plan to move older backups to cold storage and copy them to the DR Region. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Continuous replication protects against Regional outages but copies corruption and deletes, so point-in-time backups are still needed
Backups moved to cold storage can then be copied cross-Region with AWS Backup at a lower cost
A backup strategy is not proven until restores are tested and timed against the RTO
Each AWS Backup cross-Region copy is a full copy, so copying daily is expensive
questions.explanation: AWS guidance says even active/active designs need point-in-time backups, because replication faithfully copies data corruption and deletion. Backups are only trustworthy once restores are tested. AWS Backup does not support cross-Region copies of cold-storage backups, and only the first copy is full; later ones are incremental.
rationales: Correct. Replication is not a substitute for point-in-time backups.
Cold-storage backups do not support cross-Region copy. Copy first, then transition.
Correct. Restore testing is what turns a backup into a recovery capability.
Only the first copy is full; subsequent copies are incremental.

sources.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud — AWS Whitepapers
Cross-Region backup — AWS Backup Developer Guide

questions.scenario: Choosing a DR strategy
questions.stem: A small company wants to recover from the loss of its primary Region in under an hour with at most a few minutes of data loss, while keeping DR spending as low as possible. Its application tier can be launched from IaC in about 20 minutes. Which DR strategy fits best?
options: Backup and restore with nightly snapshots copied to the DR Region
Multi-site active/active with full capacity in both Regions
Pilot light: replicate the data continuously to the DR Region, keep app servers off, and launch them from IaC during failover
Rely on Multi-AZ inside the primary Region
questions.explanation: Pilot light keeps the data live in the recovery Region, which meets a minutes-level RPO, while leaving app servers switched off to keep cost low. Launching the app tier from IaC fits inside the one-hour RTO. Nightly snapshots cannot meet the RPO, active/active costs far more than needed, and Multi-AZ does not survive a Regional loss.
rationales: Nightly snapshots allow up to a day of data loss, which breaks the RPO.
This meets the targets but at the highest cost, which the company wants to avoid.
Correct. Live data plus switched-off compute matches the targets at modest cost.
Multi-AZ protects against a zone failure, not the loss of the whole Region.

sources.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud — AWS Whitepapers
Disaster recovery objectives — AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

questions.scenario: Errors during deploys
questions.stem: A service runs four instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Every rolling deploy produces a burst of 502 errors. Logs show the old instances exit within milliseconds of receiving SIGTERM. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add two more instances so each deploy affects a smaller share of traffic
Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, fail the health check, finish in-flight requests, then exit, with a deregistration delay long enough for requests to drain
Disable load balancer health checks during deploys
Switch the Dockerfile to a shell-form ENTRYPOINT so the shell handles signals
questions.explanation: The errors come from instances dying with requests still in flight. Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM plus connection draining (the target group deregistration delay) lets existing requests finish while new ones go to healthy targets. More instances only shrink the blast radius, and disabling health checks sends traffic to broken targets.
rationales: This reduces the share of failing requests but does not stop them.
Correct. Graceful shutdown with connection draining removes the dropped requests.
Health checks are what keep traffic away from unready targets.
Shell form makes it worse: the app is not PID 1 and never sees SIGTERM.

questions.scenario: Slow container stops
questions.stem: A Node.js image uses `ENTRYPOINT node server.js`. In Docker Compose, `docker compose stop` always takes about 10 seconds, and open requests are cut off. The app has a correct SIGTERM handler. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: The default STOPSIGNAL is SIGKILL; set STOPSIGNAL SIGTERM
The image has no HEALTHCHECK, so Compose cannot tell when the app is done
The grace period is too short; set stop_grace_period to 60s
The app runs under /bin/sh -c and is not PID 1, so it never receives SIGTERM and is killed after the 10s grace period; use the exec form ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]
questions.explanation: Shell-form ENTRYPOINT runs the command under /bin/sh -c, so the shell is PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM to the app. Compose waits its default stop_grace_period of 10 seconds and then sends SIGKILL. The exec form makes the app PID 1 so its handler runs.
rationales: STOPSIGNAL already defaults to SIGTERM.
HEALTHCHECK reports health; it has nothing to do with stop signals.
A longer grace period only delays the SIGKILL; the app still never sees SIGTERM.
Correct. Exec form lets the app receive SIGTERM and drain.

questions.scenario: Cascading restarts
questions.stem: A Kubernetes Deployment's liveness probe calls `/health`, which runs a query against the database. During a 30-second database failover, every pod restarts at once and the service is down for several minutes after the database is back. What change best prevents this?
options: Make liveness check only that the process can respond, and put the dependency check in the readiness probe so pods stop receiving traffic without restarting
Increase the liveness probe timeout so it waits for the database
Remove all probes so Kubernetes never restarts pods
Add a startup probe that checks the database
questions.explanation: A failed liveness probe restarts the container, while a failed readiness probe only removes the pod from Service endpoints. Tying liveness to the database turns a brief dependency blip into a fleet-wide restart. A process-only liveness check with dependency checks in readiness keeps pods warm and lets them rejoin as soon as the database returns.
rationales: Correct. Readiness takes pods out of rotation without restarting them.
A longer timeout still restarts every pod if the outage outlasts it.
With no probes, truly stuck pods are never replaced and unready pods get traffic.
Startup probes only gate the start of the container; they do not address restarts during an outage.

questions.scenario: Uptime on a budget
questions.stem: A startup runs its web app on one large VM in one Availability Zone, with a managed database. Most outages last year were caused by deploys and by the VM being rebooted for patches. Which two changes give the biggest availability gain for the money? (Select two.)
options: Run at least two smaller instances in different Availability Zones behind a load balancer with health checks
Add an active/active deployment in a second Region
Make deploys rolling and health-gated, with graceful shutdown and connection draining
Move to a single larger VM with more CPU and memory
questions.explanation: The outages came from a single point of failure and from disruptive deploys. Two instances across zones behind a health-checked load balancer survive reboots and zone issues, and rolling, health-gated deploys with draining remove deploy downtime. A second Region costs far more and does not fix deploy-induced outages, and a bigger VM is still one VM.
rationales: Correct. This removes the single instance as a point of failure.
Multi-Region costs far more and does not address the causes seen.
Correct. Zero-downtime deploys address the most common cause.
A larger VM still goes down for every reboot and deploy.

questions.scenario: Wildcard certificate
questions.stem: A team wants a single Let's Encrypt certificate for `*.example.com`. Their ACME client currently uses HTTP-01. What must they change?
options: Nothing; HTTP-01 supports wildcards if port 80 is open
Switch to the TLS-ALPN-01 challenge on port 443
Switch to the DNS-01 challenge, publishing a TXT record (optionally delegated with a CNAME)
Request the wildcard by email validation
questions.explanation: Let's Encrypt issues wildcard certificates only with the DNS-01 challenge. HTTP-01 and TLS-ALPN-01 cannot be used for wildcards. DNS-01 validation can be delegated to another zone with a CNAME or NS record.
rationales: HTTP-01 cannot validate wildcard names.
TLS-ALPN-01 also cannot issue wildcards.
Correct. DNS-01 is required for wildcards.
Let's Encrypt does not offer email validation.

questions.scenario: Hardcoded renewals
questions.stem: A team's servers renew Let's Encrypt certificates with a cron job that runs every 60 days. It has worked for years. Which change best protects them as certificate lifetimes change?
options: Request 365-day certificates through a certificate profile so renewals become rare
Use an ACME client with ARI (RFC 9773), or renew at about two-thirds of the current lifetime, and alert on certificate expiry from their own monitoring
Rely on Let's Encrypt expiration emails as a backstop
Enable OCSP stapling so clients accept certificates slightly past expiry
questions.explanation: Let's Encrypt has announced classic certificates will move from 90 to 64 days in 2027 and 45 days in 2028, so a fixed 60-day schedule will let certificates expire. ARI lets the CA signal when to renew; otherwise renew at about two-thirds of lifetime. Lifetimes cannot be adjusted per request, and expiration emails and the OCSP service have both ended.
rationales: Lifetimes cannot be adjusted, and no profile offers a year.
Correct. ARI or two-thirds-of-lifetime renewal survives the schedule changes.
Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiration emails in 2025.
OCSP has ended at Let's Encrypt, and no stapling makes an expired certificate valid.

questions.scenario: Turning on HSTS
questions.stem: A company wants HSTS on `example.com`. Most subdomains serve HTTPS, but an internal reporting tool on `reports.example.com` still uses plain HTTP. What is the safest rollout?
options: Send `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload` immediately and submit the domain to the preload list
Rely on an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect alone, since it already protects the first request
Send the HSTS header on HTTP responses so browsers learn it sooner
Fix the HTTP-only subdomain first, start with a short max-age such as 86400, then raise max-age and add includeSubDomains, and consider preload last
questions.explanation: OWASP recommends testing HSTS with a short max-age before moving to the long value, because includeSubDomains would break any subdomain that cannot do HTTPS. Preload is effectively permanent, so it comes last. A redirect alone leaves the plaintext request open to stripping, and browsers ignore HSTS sent over HTTP.
rationales: This would immediately break the HTTP-only subdomain, and preload is hard to undo.
A redirect does not stop an attacker from intercepting the plaintext request.
Browsers only honour HSTS received over HTTPS.
Correct. A staged rollout avoids locking users out of subdomains.

questions.scenario: Login abuse
questions.stem: A small SaaS behind Amazon CloudFront and an Application Load Balancer sees bursts of credential-stuffing traffic on `/login` from thousands of rotating IPs. The team wants mitigation this week without changing application code. What is the best first step?
options: Attach AWS WAF to the CloudFront distribution with managed rules and a rate-based rule on /login, and restrict the origin so it accepts traffic only via CloudFront
Add security group rules that deny the offending IP addresses
Lower the DNS TTL so traffic can be moved quickly
Scale the application to twice as many instances
questions.explanation: AWS WAF attaches to CloudFront and filters requests with managed rule groups and rate-based rules, which suit high-volume abuse from many addresses. Locking the origin to the CDN stops attackers bypassing the WAF. Security groups only allow traffic and cannot hold thousands of changing IPs, and scaling simply pays to serve the attack.
rationales: Correct. Edge filtering with rate limits fits without code changes.
Security groups have allow rules only, and blocking rotating IPs by hand does not scale.
DNS TTL changes do nothing to filter malicious requests.
More capacity absorbs the traffic but does not stop account takeover attempts.

questions.scenario: Apex domain
questions.stem: A team wants `example.com` (the zone apex, hosted in Route 53) to point at an Application Load Balancer. Their first attempt, a CNAME record at the apex, is rejected. What should they use?
options: An A record with the load balancer's current IP addresses
A TXT record containing the load balancer's DNS name
A Route 53 alias record pointing at the load balancer
A CAA record naming the load balancer
questions.explanation: DNS does not allow a CNAME at the zone apex, so Route 53 provides alias records that can point an apex name at AWS resources such as load balancers. Load balancer IP addresses change, so hardcoding them in an A record breaks. TXT and CAA records do not route traffic.
rationales: Load balancer IPs change over time, so this will eventually break.
TXT records hold text such as verification tokens; they do not route traffic.
Correct. Alias records work at the apex and follow the load balancer.
CAA records restrict which CAs may issue certificates.
