questions.scenario: Provenance for images
questions.stem: A platform team wants container images built in GitHub Actions to carry signed provenance that meets SLSA Build L3, and wants production deploys to reject images without it. What should they do?
options: Have each developer sign images locally with a personal key before pushing
Build in a shared reusable workflow that runs actions/attest with the image name and digest, and run `gh attestation verify` in the deploy job before deploying
Add actions/attest to each repository's own build workflow and trust whatever reaches the registry
Tag every image with the Git commit SHA so its origin is traceable
questions.explanation: GitHub artifact attestations meet SLSA Build L2, and Build L3 when the build runs in a shared reusable workflow, which isolates signing from user-defined steps. Provenance only becomes a control when deploys verify it, for example with gh attestation verify. Developer-signed images are forgeable provenance, and tags are mutable labels, not attestations.
rationales: Locally generated signatures do not prove what the build platform did, which is at most L1-style provenance.
Correct. A shared reusable workflow reaches L3, and verification enforces it.
Per-repo attestations reach L2, and without verification at deploy time they are not enforced.
A tag records nothing verifiable about how the image was built.

questions.scenario: Dependabot tuning
questions.stem: A team finds Dependabot noisy: dozens of small npm PRs each week, and once they merged a malicious package version within hours of its release. They still want security fixes as fast as possible. Which two `dependabot.yml` changes address this? (Select two.)
options: Use `groups` to bundle minor and patch updates into fewer pull requests
Change `schedule.interval` to `yearly`
Set a `cooldown` so version updates wait some days after a release, knowing security updates are not delayed by it
Turn off Dependabot security updates so only grouped version updates arrive
questions.explanation: Groups bundle related updates into one PR, which cuts noise. Cooldown delays version updates until a release has aged a set number of days (3 by default), which avoids adopting a brand-new malicious or broken version, and it does not delay security updates. A yearly schedule leaves dependencies stale, and disabling security updates is the opposite of the goal.
rationales: Correct. Groups reduce the number of PRs.
A yearly schedule lets dependencies fall far behind.
Correct. Cooldown targets brand-new releases while security fixes still flow.
This removes the fast security fixes the team wants.

questions.scenario: Where is the SBOM?
questions.stem: After a new OpenSSL CVE, a security engineer asks for the SBOM of last week's images. The team builds with `docker buildx build --push` and default settings, and finds a provenance attestation but no SBOM. Why, and what is the fix?
options: SBOMs are only produced by --provenance=mode=max; switch to that
Registries strip SBOMs on push; store them in the repository instead
Pinning the base image by digest generates an SBOM; pin it
Provenance is attached by default but the SBOM is opt-in; add --sbom=true to the build
questions.explanation: BuildKit attaches minimal provenance by default, while SBOM attestations must be requested with --sbom=true. mode=max adds detail to provenance, not an SBOM. Digest pinning improves reproducibility but does not list the packages inside the image.
rationales: mode=max controls provenance detail; it does not generate an SBOM.
Attestations are pushed with the image; nothing indicates the registry stripped one.
Digest pinning fixes the base image version but produces no inventory.
Correct. SBOM generation is opt-in.

questions.scenario: Patching a base image
questions.stem: A scanner flags a critical CVE in an OS library in the production image. The Dockerfile pins its base image by digest, and the base image publisher has released a fixed version. What is the right way to patch?
options: Update the pinned digest (for example via a Dependabot docker PR), rebuild with --pull, and ship the new image through the normal pipeline
Run `docker exec <container> apt-get upgrade` on each running container
Remove the digest pin and use the `latest` tag so future builds get fixes automatically
Wait for the next feature release, since rebuilding without code changes is wasteful
questions.explanation: Containers are patched by rebuilding from a fixed base image and redeploying, which keeps the registry image, the running containers and the audit trail consistent. Docker's best practices recommend pinning by digest, letting Dependabot bump it, and rebuilding with --pull. Changes made with exec are lost on restart, and floating tags make builds unreproducible.
rationales: Correct. Rebuild and redeploy through the pipeline.
The fix disappears when the container restarts, and the registry image stays vulnerable.
Floating tags trade one problem for unreproducible builds.
A critical CVE should not wait for a feature release.

questions.scenario: Production access
questions.stem: Five engineers each have an IAM user with long-lived access keys and AdministratorAccess in the production AWS account, used mainly to read logs and occasionally fix incidents. Which change best applies least privilege without blocking incident response?
options: Keep the IAM users but rotate their access keys every 90 days
Replace them with one shared admin IAM user protected by MFA
Federate through IAM Identity Center with MFA and temporary credentials, give a read-only role by default, and keep a time-limited, logged break-glass admin role for incidents
Attach a service control policy that grants read-only access to engineers
questions.explanation: AWS recommends federation with temporary credentials and MFA for people, and least-privilege permissions refined with IAM Access Analyzer. A read-only default with a logged break-glass role preserves incident response while removing standing admin keys. Rotation keeps full admin rights, a shared user destroys attribution, and SCPs never grant permissions.
rationales: Rotation shortens key lifetime but leaves standing admin privilege.
Shared credentials make audit logs useless for attributing actions.
Correct. Temporary, scoped access with an audited escalation path.
SCPs only limit permissions; they grant nothing.

sources.title: Security best practices in IAM — AWS IAM User Guide

questions.scenario: Who deleted it?
questions.stem: After an incident in which nobody could tell who deleted a security group, the team wants a long-term record of AWS API activity that stays safe even if a production admin account is compromised. What should they set up?
options: Rely on application logs on the EC2 instances
Create an organization CloudTrail trail that delivers to an S3 bucket in a separate log-archive account that production admins cannot modify
Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnets
Increase CloudWatch metric retention for EC2
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records AWS API activity, including who called DeleteSecurityGroup and from where, and a trail delivers those events to S3 for long-term retention. Delivering to a separate log-archive account keeps an attacker with production admin rights from deleting the evidence. Flow logs record network traffic, not API calls, and metrics carry no identity.
rationales: Application logs do not see AWS control-plane API calls.
Correct. A trail into an isolated account gives durable, tamper-resistant audit logs.
Flow logs record packets between addresses, not who changed resources.
Metrics have no record of which identity made an API call.

questions.scenario: A two-person startup runs one small API in private subnets on AWS. The monthly bill is far higher than the compute estimate. Cost Explorer shows the largest line items are a NAT gateway (hourly and data processing) and EC2-Other. The API mostly reads and writes objects in S3 in the same Region.
questions.stem: Which change most directly reduces the cost without changing the application?
options: Buy a 3-year Compute Savings Plan for the NAT gateway hours.
Move the S3 bucket to a different Region to spread the load.
Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and route the private subnets' S3 traffic through it.
Increase the API instance size so requests finish faster.
questions.explanation: Traffic from private subnets to S3 through a NAT gateway pays the per-GB processing charge. S3 gateway endpoints are free, and same-Region EC2-to-S3 transfer is free, so routing S3 traffic through the endpoint removes most of that charge.
rationales: Savings Plans cover compute (EC2, Fargate, Lambda), not NAT gateway charges.
Cross-Region access adds transfer charges instead of removing them.
Correct: gateway endpoints for S3 have no charge and bypass NAT processing fees.
A bigger instance raises compute cost and does nothing for NAT data processing.

questions.scenario: You estimate an AWS Lambda function: 10 million requests per month, 200 ms average duration, 512 MB memory, x86, ZIP package on a managed runtime.
questions.stem: Which statement about the estimate is correct?
options: The function uses 1,000,000 GB-seconds per month, and the bill is requests plus GB-seconds beyond the monthly free tier.
Only duration is billed; requests are free after the first million forever.
Memory does not affect cost; only the number of requests does.
Lambda bills per started minute, so each 200 ms request is billed as 60 seconds.
questions.explanation: 10M requests x 0.2 s x 0.5 GB is 1,000,000 GB-s. Lambda bills a per-million-request fee plus duration in GB-seconds, after the monthly free tier of 1M requests and 400,000 GB-s. With current x86 rates this comes to roughly USD 12 per month.
rationales: Correct: GB-seconds equal memory times duration, and both requests and duration are billed beyond the free tier.
Requests are billed per million beyond the free tier; they are not free indefinitely.
Duration is billed in GB-seconds, so memory directly scales cost.
Lambda duration is metered in fine increments, not per minute.

questions.scenario: A team set an AWS Budget of USD 200 per month with an alert at 100% of actual spend. A misconfigured job ran overnight and the month closed at USD 900. The alert email arrived the next morning, after most of the damage.
questions.stem: Which improvements address what went wrong? (Select two.)
options: Add a forecasted-spend alert at a lower threshold, such as 80%, so the alert fires earlier.
Rely on the budget as a hard cap; it should have stopped the job at USD 200.
Attach a budget action that applies a deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed, and add usage-level guards (for example concurrency or instance limits) on the job.
Increase the budget to USD 1,000 so the alert does not fire.
questions.explanation: Budgets are not a hard cap: billing data refreshes up to three times a day, so spend can keep rising before notification. Forecasted alerts at a lower threshold warn earlier, and budget actions (such as applying a deny IAM policy) plus resource limits reduce the blast radius.
rationales: Correct: forecasted alerts at a lower threshold give earlier warning.
Budgets notify and can trigger actions, but they do not cap spend, and data lags by hours.
Correct: budget actions can apply a deny policy, and resource limits bound runaway usage.
Raising the threshold hides the problem instead of controlling it.

questions.scenario: You added tags `app` and `env` to every resource through Terraform default tags two days ago. In Cost Explorer, you cannot group or filter by either tag.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: Cost Explorer only supports AWS-generated tags.
The tags have not been activated as cost allocation tags in the Billing console.
Tags only work on EC2 instances.
Tags must be applied by hand in the console to count for billing.
questions.explanation: User-defined tags must be activated as cost allocation tags (from the management account or a standalone account) before they appear in Cost Explorer and the cost allocation report. After activation they can take up to 24 hours to show.
rationales: User-defined tags are supported once activated.
Correct: tags must be activated before billing tools can use them.
Cost allocation tags apply across many resource types, such as S3 buckets and EC2 instances.
How a tag is applied does not matter; activation does.

questions.scenario: A three-person team runs EC2 and Fargate today and expects to move some workloads to Lambda in the next year. Usage has a steady baseline plus daytime peaks. They want a commitment discount.
questions.stem: Which approach is best?
options: Buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the full peak usage of the current instance family.
Buy a 3-year all-upfront commitment for peak usage to get the largest discount.
Right-size first, then buy a Compute Savings Plan covering only the steady baseline.
Avoid commitments; on-demand is always cheaper for small teams.
questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2 (any family or Region), Fargate and Lambda, so they survive the planned architecture change. Committing only to the right-sized baseline avoids paying for commitment that peaks or future changes would leave unused.
rationales: An instance-family plan does not follow workloads to Fargate or Lambda, and committing to peak wastes money off-peak.
A peak-sized commitment is underused most of the day regardless of upfront payment.
Correct: flexible coverage and a baseline-sized commitment match the situation.
For a predictable baseline, a commitment discount is usually cheaper than on-demand.

questions.scenario: An internal admin tool on AWS gets a few hundred requests during business hours and none at night or on weekends. It runs on two always-on EC2 instances behind a load balancer.
questions.stem: Which change most reduces cost while keeping the tool available?
options: Move it to a scale-to-zero platform such as Lambda or Cloud Run with no minimum instances, accepting occasional cold starts.
Buy a 3-year Savings Plan for the two instances.
Add a third instance for redundancy.
Keep the instances and add provisioned concurrency.
questions.explanation: With long idle periods, the biggest waste is paying for capacity that serves nothing. Scale-to-zero platforms charge little or nothing when idle and stay within free tiers at this volume; the cost is a cold start on the first request after idle.
rationales: Correct: scale to zero removes idle cost for a low, bursty workload.
A commitment discounts idle capacity but still pays for it around the clock.
More instances increase idle cost.
Provisioned concurrency is a Lambda feature and adds always-on cost; it does not apply to EC2.

questions.scenario: You want evidence before resizing several EC2 instances, an Auto Scaling group and some ECS services on Fargate that you suspect are oversized.
questions.stem: Which AWS service is designed to produce rightsizing and idle-resource recommendations from utilization data?
options: AWS Budgets
Savings Plans recommendations in the purchase flow
Cost allocation tags
AWS Compute Optimizer
questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer is an opt-in service that analyzes configuration and CloudWatch utilization (14 days by default) to recommend rightsizing and identify idle resources for EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate, RDS and more.
rationales: Budgets track spend against thresholds; they do not recommend resource sizes.
Commitment recommendations size a discount purchase, not the resources themselves.
Tags attribute cost; they do not analyze utilization.
Correct: Compute Optimizer produces rightsizing and idle recommendations.

questions.scenario: A solo developer is launching a new containerized web API on AWS in late 2026 and wants the least operational work: no cluster management, built-in load balancing and auto scaling.

options: AWS App Runner, the simplest AWS container PaaS.
Amazon ECS Express Mode, which provisions an ECS service on Fargate with a load balancer and auto scaling.
A self-managed Kubernetes cluster on EC2.
A single EC2 instance with Docker installed and a cron job to restart containers.

rationales: App Runner is closed to new customers.
Correct: Express Mode is the recommended simple path for managed containers on AWS.
Self-managed Kubernetes adds the most operational work for one person.
A hand-run VM means patching, restarts and scaling are all your job.

questions.scenario: A team of two is choosing a platform for three HTTP services with moderate, variable traffic. One teammate proposes managed Kubernetes "so we can grow into it." Neither has run Kubernetes in production.
questions.stem: What is the strongest argument for a managed container platform (such as Cloud Run or ECS on Fargate) instead?
options: Kubernetes cannot run HTTP services.
Kubernetes has no autoscaling.
Managed container platforms remove cluster upgrades and add-on management, and the same container images can move to Kubernetes later if needed.
Managed container platforms are always cheaper than any Kubernetes setup at every scale.
questions.explanation: For a tiny team the main cost of Kubernetes is operational: frequent minor releases (only the newest three lines are supported), add-ons, networking and the control plane. A managed container platform avoids that, and because the unit is a container image, migrating later stays possible.
rationales: Kubernetes runs HTTP services routinely.
Kubernetes supports autoscaling.
Correct: less to operate now, with portability preserved through containers.
Cost depends on workload; "always cheaper" is not defensible.

questions.scenario: A nightly report job is being moved to AWS Lambda. Today it takes about 40 minutes on one VM.
questions.stem: What is the main problem with running it as a single Lambda invocation?
options: The maximum Lambda timeout is 15 minutes, so the job must be split into chunks or run as a container task instead.
Lambda cannot be scheduled.
Lambda cannot read from a database.
Lambda only supports synchronous invocations.
questions.explanation: Lambda functions can run for at most 900 seconds. A 40-minute job must be broken into smaller units (for example fan-out through a queue or an orchestration service) or run on a container platform such as Fargate.
rationales: Correct: the 900-second timeout rules out a single 40-minute run.
Lambda can be invoked on a schedule.
Lambda can connect to databases.
Lambda supports asynchronous invocations too.

questions.scenario: During a marketing spike, an image-processing Lambda function scaled out heavily. At the same time, the checkout API (also Lambda, same account and Region) started returning throttling errors.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The checkout function ran out of memory; double its memory.
Cold starts caused the throttles; add a warm-up cron job.
The checkout responses exceeded Lambda's 6 MB synchronous payload limit; compress responses.
Both functions share the account's Regional concurrency limit; set reserved concurrency to guarantee checkout capacity and cap the image function.
questions.explanation: The default concurrency limit applies per Region and is shared by all functions in the account. A function that scales out can consume it and starve others. Reserved concurrency guarantees a function's share and also caps it.
rationales: Memory exhaustion produces errors in the function, not throttling across functions.
Cold starts add latency; they do not cause throttling errors.
Payload limits cause invocation errors for oversized requests or responses, not throttling of one function while another scales out.
Correct: shared Regional concurrency explains cross-function throttling; reserved concurrency isolates them.

questions.scenario: A customer-facing API on Lambda has a p99 latency problem after quiet periods. Initialization loads a large SDK and ML model. Traffic is spiky and the team is cost-sensitive.
questions.stem: Which actions reduce cold-start impact? (Select two.)
options: Trim the deployment package and lazily load the rarely used model only on the code paths that need it.
Enable provisioned concurrency sized to the baseline traffic, accepting that it bills while idle.
Increase the function timeout to 900 seconds.
Move the initialization code into the handler so it runs on every request.
questions.explanation: Smaller packages and lazy loading shorten INIT, which also matters for cost because INIT is now billed for ZIP-packaged managed runtimes. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized, at the price of an always-on charge.
rationales: Correct: less work during initialization means shorter cold starts.
Correct: provisioned concurrency removes cold starts for the warm capacity, at extra cost.
The timeout limits run time; it does not speed up initialization.
Running setup on every request makes every request slower.

questions.scenario: An I/O-bound API on Cloud Run spends most of each request waiting on a database. While debugging months ago, someone set maximum concurrent requests per instance to 1 and never reverted it. Under load, the service now runs many instances and the bill is rising.
questions.stem: Which setting is most likely to reduce instance count without code changes?
options: Keep concurrency at 1 and give each instance more CPU.
Increase minimum instances to 50.
Raise per-instance concurrency back to the default (80) or higher so each instance serves many waiting requests at once.
Write responses to the local filesystem as a cache.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run instances can handle many concurrent requests (default 80, maximum 1,000). A concurrency of 1 forces one instance per in-flight request; for I/O-bound work, restoring higher concurrency lets fewer instances serve the same load, cutting cost.
rationales: With concurrency 1, each in-flight request still needs its own instance; more CPU per instance does not help I/O-bound waits and raises the per-instance cost.
More minimum instances raise idle cost.
Correct: higher concurrency lets one instance serve many requests that are waiting on I/O, so fewer instances are needed.
The filesystem is in memory and lost when instances stop; it is a poor cache and uses instance memory.

questions.scenario: A service on Lambda now handles steady, high traffic 24 hours a day, every day. Its monthly Lambda bill has grown well past the cost of an equivalent always-on container.
questions.stem: What is the most reasonable next step?
options: Re-estimate with current pricing and consider moving the hot path to a right-sized container on Fargate or Cloud Run, possibly covered by a commitment discount.
Stay on Lambda; serverless is always cheapest because you never pay for idle.
Rewrite the service in a different language to reduce request count.
Increase memory to the maximum to finish requests faster.
questions.explanation: Per-request pricing shines for spiky or low traffic. When utilization is steady and high, a right-sized always-on container can be cheaper, and Compute Savings Plans can cover Fargate as well as Lambda. Keeping logic behind a thin handler makes this move easier.
rationales: Correct: re-estimate and move the steady path where the economics favor it.
Serverless is not always cheapest; at steady high load per-GB-second billing can cost more.
Language choice does not change request count.
More memory raises GB-second cost and only sometimes shortens duration enough to compensate.

questions.scenario: A team worries about lock-in before building on a functions platform.
questions.stem: Which practice best reduces vendor coupling while still using serverless?
options: Put all business logic inside provider-specific event handler signatures.
Deploy to two providers at once from day one.
Avoid managed services entirely and run your own message broker on a VM.
Keep business logic in plain modules behind a thin handler, and use standard interfaces such as HTTP and container images at the edges.
questions.explanation: Coupling mostly comes from event formats, triggers, IAM and surrounding managed services. Isolating logic behind a thin adapter and using portable interfaces keeps migration cost low without giving up the benefits of the platform.
rationales: Spreading provider event shapes through the codebase maximizes coupling.
Running on two providers from the start doubles operational work for a hypothetical benefit.
Self-hosting adds operations and cost for a small team.
Correct: a thin adapter plus standard interfaces limits what a move would touch.

questions.scenario: A three-person team will create about six small services over the next year. Each new service so far took two days to set up CI, Docker, logging and deployment.
questions.stem: Which investment gives the best return first?
options: Build a self-hosted developer portal with a service catalog before writing the next service.
Create one golden path: a template repository plus a reusable CI/CD workflow and an IaC module for the standard service.
Let each service choose its own tools so nobody is constrained.
Hire a dedicated platform team.
questions.explanation: Platform guidance recommends starting with a thinnest viable platform and paving paths incrementally. For a small team, a template, a reusable workflow and a module remove most of the repeated setup without a large up-front build.
rationales: A portal is a big up-front effort that does not by itself remove the repeated setup.
Correct: a minimal golden path directly removes the two-day setup.
Unconstrained choices multiply the setup and operations burden.
A platform team is out of proportion for three people.

questions.scenario: Your team created five service repositories from a GitHub template repository that included a full CI workflow file. You fixed a security issue in the template's workflow, but the five services still run the old version.
questions.stem: Which changes prevent this drift in the future? (Select two.)
options: Move the shared CI logic into a reusable workflow called with workflow_call, so services reference one maintained definition.
Expect template fixes to propagate automatically and wait for GitHub to sync them.
Version the shared workflow and IaC modules, and have services pin and upgrade versions deliberately.
Fork the template repository for each service instead, so template fixes reach the services automatically.
questions.explanation: A repository created from a template is an independent copy with its own history, so template edits never flow into it. Keeping shared logic in reusable workflows and versioned modules means a fix is made once and adopted through a version bump.
rationales: Correct: a reusable workflow centralizes the logic that was copied.
Template-created repositories do not sync with the template.
Correct: versioned shared components make upgrades explicit and repeatable.
Forks do not update automatically either (they must be synced by hand), and forks are meant for contributing back to one project, not for running many independent services; this does not solve drift.

questions.scenario: A small team is deciding which manual task to automate next. Candidates: (a) a deploy and rollback procedure done several times a week with a 10-step checklist, (b) a yearly certificate audit, (c) renaming old Slack channels.
questions.stem: Which should they automate first, and why?
options: The deploy and rollback procedure, because it is frequent, error-prone and on the critical path.
The yearly audit, because audits are important.
Slack channel renaming, because it is easy.
None; automation never pays off for small teams.
questions.explanation: Automation pays off fastest for work that is manual, repetitive, error-prone and on the critical path (the traits of toil in the Google SRE book). The deploy path meets all of these; a yearly task is better served by a checklist.
rationales: Correct: frequency, error rate and criticality make the deploy path the best target.
A yearly task gives little return on automation effort; a checklist suffices.
Easy but low-value automation does not reduce meaningful toil.
Small teams benefit most from removing repeated manual work.

questions.scenario: You are estimating the monthly cost of a tiny always-on API on AWS: one Fargate task, one Application Load Balancer, one NAT gateway, and two public IPv4 addresses.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the likely shape of the bill?
options: Only the Fargate task costs money; networking pieces are free when traffic is low.
NAT gateways are billed only per GB, so they cost nothing at low traffic.
Public IPv4 addresses are free while attached to a running resource.
Fixed hourly charges for the load balancer, NAT gateway and public IPv4 addresses can equal or exceed the cost of the small task itself.
questions.explanation: A small Fargate task costs on the order of USD 10 per month, while a NAT gateway has an hourly charge (about USD 33 per month idle at the example rate) plus per-GB processing, an Application Load Balancer bills per hour plus capacity units, and public IPv4 addresses bill hourly whether used or idle. For small apps, plumbing often dominates.
rationales: NAT gateways, load balancers and public IPv4 addresses all have hourly charges.
NAT gateways have both an hourly charge and a per-GB charge.
Public IPv4 addresses are billed hourly whether in use or idle.
Correct: idle plumbing is a large share of a small bill.
